# Lines format (one JSON object per line) - common in big data

# Save

df.to_json("output.jsonl", orient="records", lines=True)

# data = [{"id": 1, "address": {"city": "NYC", "zip": "10001"}}, ...]

df = pd.json_normalize(data)
# Flattens to columns: id, address.city, address.zip

df = pd.json_normalize(data, sep="_") # use _ instead of .

Parquet - the big-data format

# Need pyarrow: pip install pyarrow

# Parquet stores data in columnar format - much faster than CSV for big files
# Also preserves dtypes (CSV loses them)

# Save (much smaller file than CSV, faster to read)
df.to_parquet("data.parquet")

# Read
df = pd.read_parquet("data.parquet")

# Read only specific columns - reads less from disk
df = pd.read_parquet("data.parquet", columns=["id", "amount"])

# Compression options (default is snappy)
df.to_parquet("data.parquet", compression="gzip") # smaller, slower

# Why parquet > CSV for analysis:
# - 5-10x smaller
# - 5-50x faster to read
# - Preserves int/float/datetime types
# - Supports nested data
# - Reads only needed columns

Other formats

# SQL (covered more in ch10)
import sqlalchemy
engine = sqlalchemy.create_engine("sqlite:///mydb.db")

df.to_sql("results", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False)

Selection is what you do most in pandas - filter rows, pick columns, slice and dice. Understanding loc/iloc/boolean masks deeply means writing code that's both correct and fast.

.loc - label-based selection

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
 "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave"],
 "age": [30, 25, 35, 28],
 "city": ["NYC", "SF", "NYC", "LA"],
}, index=["a", "b", "c", "d"])

# Single row - returns a Series
df.loc["a"]

# Multiple rows
df.loc[["a", "c"]]

# Slice - INCLUSIVE on both ends
df.loc["a":"c"] # rows a, b, c

# Single cell
df.loc["a", "name"] # 'Alice'

# Row + column subset
df.loc[["a", "b"], ["name", "age"]]

# All rows, specific columns
df.loc[:, "name":"age"] # name and age columns

# Boolean mask + columns
df.loc[df["age"] > 27, ["name", "city"]]

# Setting values - very common
df.loc[df["age"] > 30, "category"] = "senior"
df.loc["a", "name"] = "Alicia"

.iloc - position-based selection

# Same as Python list/NumPy indexing - 0-indexed, exclusive slice
df.iloc[0] # first row
df.iloc[-1] # last row
df.iloc[0:2] # first 2 rows (NOT inclusive of end)
df.iloc[[0, 2]] # rows 0 and 2

# Cell
df.iloc[0, 0] # first row, first column

# Subset
df.iloc[0:2, 1:3] # first 2 rows, cols 1-2
df.iloc[:, 0] # all rows, first column -> Series
df.iloc[:, [0, 2]] # all rows, cols 0 and 2

# Negative indexing works
df.iloc[-3:] # last 3 rows

Boolean masking - the core of filtering

# Single condition
df[df["age"] > 30]
df.loc[df["age"] > 30] # equivalent, more explicit

# Multiple conditions - use & | ~ with PARENTHESES
df[(df["age"] > 25) & (df["city"] == "NYC")]
df[(df["age"] < 25) | (df["age"] > 35)]
df[~(df["city"] == "NYC")] # negation - same as !=

# Membership test
df[df["city"].isin(["NYC", "LA"])]
df[~df["city"].isin(["NYC", "LA"])] # NOT in NYC or LA

# Between
df[df["age"].between(25, 35)] # inclusive

# String matching
df[df["name"].str.startswith("A")]
df[df["name"].str.contains("ar", case=False)]
df[df["name"].str.match(r"^[AB]")] # regex

# Null checks
df[df["age"].isna()]
df[df["age"].notna()]

# Top N rows by a column
df.nlargest(3, "age")
df.nsmallest(2, "age")
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Use &/|/~ with parentheses around each condition - and/or/not won't work because they expect single bools, not Series. Forgetting parens leads to confusing errors because & binds tighter than comparisons.

query() - readable filtering with strings

# Verbose
df[(df["age"] > 25) & (df["city"] == "NYC") & (df["salary"] > 50000)]

# Same with query - much cleaner for complex filters
df.query("age > 25 and city == 'NYC' and salary > 50000")

# Variable injection with @
min_age = 30
df.query("age >= @min_age")

# Column names with spaces or hyphens - use backticks
df.query("`first name` == 'Alice'")

# In/not in
df.query("city in ['NYC', 'LA']")
df.query("city not in ['SF']")

# String operations need .str
df.query("name.str.startswith('A')") # works in newer pandas

# Performance tip: query is sometimes faster on large dfs because
# it doesn't create intermediate boolean Series

SettingWithCopyWarning - the famous pandas annoyance

# This often triggers the warning:
df_subset = df[df["age"] > 30]
df_subset["age"] = 99 # SettingWithCopyWarning
# Did you modify df or df_subset? Pandas can't tell.

# Right way 1: explicit copy
df_subset = df[df["age"] > 30].copy()
df_subset["age"] = 99 # safe - clearly a separate df

# Right way 2: chained .loc
df.loc[df["age"] > 30, "age"] = 99 # modifies df in place, no warning

# Why this happens:
# df[mask] might return a view OR a copy - depends on internals.
# Pandas warns to keep you from accidentally writing to the wrong one.
# In pandas 3.0+ the rules become stricter (Copy-on-Write).

Practical patterns

# Top-N per group
df.groupby("city").apply(lambda g: g.nlargest(3, "salary"))

# Get rows where any column is null
df[df.isna().any(axis=1)]

# Get rows where ALL of a set of columns are filled
df.dropna(subset=["age", "salary"])

# Sample rows
df.sample(10) # 10 random rows
df.sample(frac=0.1, random_state=42) # 10% sample
df.sample(n=5, weights="size") # weighted sample

# Random shuffle
df = df.sample(frac=1, random_state=42).reset_index(drop=True)

# First/last per group 
df.drop_duplicates("user_id", keep="first")
df.sort_values("date").drop_duplicates("user_id", keep="last") # last per user

Practice

Given a DataFrame of orders with columns customer_id, amount, status, date: select all shipped orders over $100 from a customer named 'C123' in 2024. Use .query() for readability.

Show solution 
import pandas as pd

# Assuming df is loaded
result = df.query(
 "customer_id == 'C123' "
 "and status == 'shipped' "
 "and amount > 100 "
 "and date >= '2024-01-01' and date < '2025-01-01'"
)

# Or with masking
mask = (
 (df["customer_id"] == "C123") &
 (df["status"] == "shipped") &
 (df["amount"] > 100) &
 (df["date"].dt.year == 2024)
)
result = df[mask]

Key terms

Boolean mask
Series of True/False used to filter rows.
isin()
Method that tests membership in a list - vectorized in.
query()
String-based filtering - cleaner than long boolean expressions.
SettingWithCopyWarning
Pandas warning when you might be modifying a copy of a slice.
nlargest / nsmallest
Get top N rows by a column without full sort.

The mental model: loc = labels, iloc = positions

Every selection confusion in pandas traces back to mixing these up. loc speaks the language of your index labels (names, dates, IDs). iloc speaks pure integer positions (0, 1, 2...) regardless of what the index looks like. They behave differently in one critical way:

df = pd.DataFrame({'price': [10, 20, 30, 40]}, index=[3, 1, 4, 2])

df.loc[3]      # row with LABEL 3 → price 10 (first row)
df.iloc[3]     # row at POSITION 3 → price 40 (last row)

# Slicing — the trap:
df.loc[3:4]    # label slice: INCLUSIVE of both ends
df.iloc[0:2]   # position slice: EXCLUSIVE of end (like Python lists)
⚠ THE INCLUSIVITY TRAP

df.loc['a':'c'] INCLUDES 'c'. df.iloc[0:3] EXCLUDES position 3. This asymmetry is intentional (label slices can't know "one past c") but bites everyone once. Memorize it now.

Boolean masking — the real workhorse

# Build conditions — each produces a True/False Series
high_price = df['price'] > 100
in_stock   = df['inventory'] > 0
on_sale    = df['discount'].notna()

# Combine with & | ~ — PARENTHESES REQUIRED
df[ (high_price) & (in_stock) ]
df[ (df['price'] > 100) & (df['inventory'] > 0) ]     # inline version
df[ ~on_sale ]                                         # ~ = NOT

# Common condition helpers
df[ df['category'].isin(['A', 'B']) ]                  # membership
df[ df['name'].str.contains('pro', case=False) ]       # string match
df[ df['date'].between('2024-01-01', '2024-06-30') ]   # range
df[ df['email'].notna() ]                              # non-null only
⚠ WHY PARENTHESES

df[df.a > 1 & df.b < 5] fails because & binds tighter than > — Python reads it as df.a > (1 & df.b) < 5. Always: df[(df.a > 1) & (df.b < 5)]. And use & | ~, never and or not (those work on single booleans, not Series).

SettingWithCopyWarning — what it actually means

# THE BUG: chained indexing
df[df['price'] > 100]['discount'] = 0.1     # ⚠ may modify a COPY — silently does nothing

# THE FIX: one .loc with both selections
df.loc[df['price'] > 100, 'discount'] = 0.1  # guaranteed to modify df

# Reading is fine either way; WRITING needs single-step .loc

The warning means pandas can't guarantee whether you're writing to the original frame or a temporary copy. The rule that makes it disappear forever: when assigning, always use one .loc[rows, cols] = value call.

query() — readable filtering for complex conditions

# These are equivalent:
df[(df['price'] > 100) & (df['qty'] < 50) & (df['region'] == 'East')]
df.query('price > 100 and qty < 50 and region == "East"')

# Variables via @
threshold = 100
df.query('price > @threshold')

query() shines when conditions pile up — it reads like English and skips the bracket noise. Slightly slower on small frames, often faster on large ones (numexpr engine).

Rows by conditionBoolean mask or query()
Rows + columns by name.loc[mask, ['col1','col2']]
First/last N rows.iloc[:n] / .iloc[-n:] (or head/tail)
Single cell, fast.at[label, col] / .iat[i, j]
Assignment with filterALWAYS .loc[mask, col] = value
✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • loc = labels (inclusive slices); iloc = positions (exclusive slices)
  • Boolean masks: parentheses around each condition; & | ~ not and/or/not
  • SettingWithCopyWarning → fix with single-step .loc[rows, cols] = value

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

GroupBy is the most powerful pandas operation. Split data by a key, apply a function to each group, combine results. Most analytical questions are groupby questions: 'avg revenue per region', 'top 5 products per category'.

The Split-Apply-Combine pattern

  • Split: divide data into groups based on some criterion.
  • Apply: run a function on each group (aggregation, transformation, or filter).
  • Combine: merge results back into one structure.
  • Three operation types: aggregate (one value per group), transform (same shape as input), filter (drop or keep entire groups).

Aggregation - one value per group

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
 "team": ["A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "C"],
 "player": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave", "Eve", "Frank"],
 "points": [25, 30, 18, 22, 28, 15],
 "rebounds": [10, 8, 5, 7, 12, 6],
})

# Average points by team
df.groupby("team")["points"].mean()
# team
# A 27.5
# B 22.7
# C 15.0

# Many aggregations at once - returns a DataFrame
df.groupby("team")[["points", "rebounds"]].mean()

# All numeric columns
df.groupby("team").mean(numeric_only=True)

# Multiple aggregations on multiple columns - .agg()
df.groupby("team").agg(
 avg_points=("points", "mean"),
 max_points=("points", "max"),
 total_rebounds=("rebounds", "sum"),
 n_players=("player", "count"),
)

# Multiple aggs per column with a list
df.groupby("team")["points"].agg(["mean", "max", "min", "count"])

# Different aggs per column
df.groupby("team").agg({
 "points": ["mean", "max"],
 "rebounds": "sum",
})

Group by multiple columns

sales = pd.DataFrame({
 "region": ["East", "East", "West", "West", "East", "West"],
 "product": ["A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "A"],
 "amount": [100, 200, 150, 300, 250, 175],
})

# Two-level grouping
sales.groupby(["region", "product"])["amount"].sum()
# region product
# East A 350
# B 200
# West A 325
# B 300

# Result has a MultiIndex - reset to columns
sales.groupby(["region", "product"], as_index=False)["amount"].sum()
# Returns a flat DataFrame instead

# Or reset_index()
result = sales.groupby(["region", "product"])["amount"].sum().reset_index()

Built-in aggregations

gb = df.groupby("team")["points"]

gb.mean()
gb.sum()
gb.count() # non-null count
gb.size() # row count (incl. nulls)
gb.min(), gb.max()
gb.median()
gb.std(), gb.var()
gb.first(), gb.last()
gb.nth(0) # first row of each group (alternative to first)
gb.nunique() # unique values per group

# Custom aggregation
gb.agg(lambda x: x.max() - x.min()) # range

# Named aggregations (Python 3.7+) - cleanest
df.groupby("team").agg(
 average=("points", "mean"),
 spread=("points", lambda x: x.max() - x.min()),
)

transform - same shape as input

# transform broadcasts result back to original rows
# Useful for "compute group stat, attach to each row"

df["team_avg"] = df.groupby("team")["points"].transform("mean")
df["pct_of_team_avg"] = df["points"] / df["team_avg"]

# Z-score within each group
df["zscore_in_team"] = df.groupby("team")["points"].transform(
 lambda x: (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
)

# Rank within group
df["rank_in_team"] = df.groupby("team")["points"].rank(ascending=False)

# Compare to: aggregate would collapse to one row per team
# Transform keeps all rows but adds group-level info

filter - keep or drop entire groups

# Keep only teams with average > 20
result = df.groupby("team").filter(lambda g: g["points"].mean() > 20)
# Returns rows from teams A and B (their averages are > 20),
# DROPS team C entirely (avg=15)

# Keep only groups with at least 2 members
df.groupby("team").filter(lambda g: len(g) >= 2)

# Keep only top-3 teams by total points
top_teams = (
 df.groupby("team")["points"].sum()
 .nlargest(3).index
)
df[df["team"].isin(top_teams)]

apply - the catch-all

# Top N rows per group
top_2_per_team = (
 df.groupby("team", group_keys=False)
 .apply(lambda g: g.nlargest(2, "points"))
)

# Same with sort_values + head per group (often faster)
top_2 = (
 df.sort_values("points", ascending=False)
 .groupby("team")
 .head(2)
)

# Custom group-level computation
def gini(values):
 """Gini coefficient - inequality metric."""
 sorted_vals = values.sort_values().values
 n = len(sorted_vals)
 cumsum = sorted_vals.cumsum()
 return (2 * (cumsum * range(1, n+1)).sum() / cumsum.sum() - (n+1)) / n

df.groupby("team")["points"].apply(gini)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

apply is general but slow - it iterates groups in Python. Prefer built-in aggregations (mean, sum) when possible. transform with a string name is also fast. Use apply only when the alternatives don't fit.

Real-world: customer cohort analysis

orders = pd.DataFrame({
 "customer_id": [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3],
 "order_date": pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-15", "2024-03-01",
 "2024-02-10", "2024-04-05", "2024-05-15",
 "2024-06-01"]),
 "amount": [100, 50, 200, 150, 75, 300],
})

# Cohort = month of first order
orders["cohort"] = orders.groupby("customer_id")["order_date"].transform("min").dt.to_period("M")

# Per-cohort metrics
cohort_summary = orders.groupby("cohort").agg(
 n_customers=("customer_id", "nunique"),
 n_orders=("customer_id", "count"),
 total_revenue=("amount", "sum"),
 avg_order=("amount", "mean"),
)

# Customer lifetime value
clv = orders.groupby("customer_id").agg(
 n_orders=("amount", "count"),
 total_spent=("amount", "sum"),
 first_order=("order_date", "min"),
 last_order=("order_date", "max"),
)
clv["days_active"] = (clv["last_order"] - clv["first_order"]).dt.days

Practice

Given a DataFrame sales with columns region, product, amount: get the top product (by total amount) within each region.

Show solution 
import pandas as pd

# Aggregate to region+product totals
totals = (
 sales.groupby(["region", "product"], as_index=False)["amount"].sum()
)

# For each region, keep the row with max amount
top_per_region = (
 totals.sort_values("amount", ascending=False)
 .drop_duplicates("region", keep="first")
)

# Or with idxmax()
idx = totals.groupby("region")["amount"].idxmax()
top_per_region = totals.loc[idx]

Key terms

GroupBy
Object representing data split by some key.
Aggregation
Reducing each group to a single value (sum, mean, etc.).
Transform
Returns same shape as input - broadcasts group stats back.
Filter
Keeps or drops entire groups based on a predicate.
apply
General group-level function; flexible but slower than built-ins.
Named aggregation
.agg(new_col=("orig_col", "func")) - cleanest syntax.

Exercise form: distinct customers per category — df.groupby("category")["customer_id"].nunique() — nunique counts DISTINCT values inside each group.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "region": np.repeat(["north", "south", "east"], 4),
    "store":  [f"s{i}" for i in range(12)],
    "sales":  [120, 90, 140, 200, 75, 160, 110, 95, 180, 130, 60, 145],
    "staff":  [4, 3, 5, 7, 2, 6, 4, 3, 6, 5, 2, 5],
})
print(df.to_string(index=False))

print("\n1. Split, apply, combine - one line.")
g = df.groupby("region")["sales"]
print(g.sum().to_string())
print(f"   groups: {dict((k, list(v)) for k, v in df.groupby('region').groups.items())}")

print("\n2. agg with a dict gives you a table, not a pile of separate results.")
out = df.groupby("region").agg(
    total_sales=("sales", "sum"),
    mean_sales=("sales", "mean"),
    best=("sales", "max"),
    stores=("store", "count"),
    staff=("staff", "sum"))
out["sales_per_head"] = (out["total_sales"] / out["staff"]).round(1)
print(out.round(1).to_string())
print("   Named aggregation (name=(column, function)) gives flat, readable column names.")

print("\n3. Without named aggregation you get a MultiIndex on the columns.")
multi = df.groupby("region").agg({"sales": ["sum", "mean"], "staff": "max"})
print(multi.round(1).to_string())
print(f"   columns are tuples now: {list(multi.columns)[:2]}...")
print(f"   flatten with: {['_'.join(c).strip('_') for c in multi.columns]}")

print("\n4. transform keeps the original shape; agg collapses it.")
df["region_total"] = df.groupby("region")["sales"].transform("sum")
df["share"] = (df["sales"] / df["region_total"] * 100).round(1)
df["rank_in_region"] = df.groupby("region")["sales"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
print(df[["region", "store", "sales", "region_total", "share", "rank_in_region"]].to_string(index=False))
print("   That is how you compare a row against its own group without a join.")

print("\n5. filter keeps whole GROUPS, not rows.")
strong = df.groupby("region").filter(lambda x: x["sales"].sum() > 450)
print(f"   regions whose total exceeds 450: {sorted(strong['region'].unique())}")
print(f"   rows kept: {len(strong)} of {len(df)}")

print("\n6. Grouping by more than one key, and getting a flat table back.")
df["tier"] = np.where(df["sales"] >= 130, "high", "low")
two = df.groupby(["region", "tier"])["sales"].sum()
print(two.to_string())
print(f"   the index is now a MultiIndex: {two.index.names}")
print("   .reset_index() turns it back into ordinary columns:")
print(two.reset_index().to_string(index=False))

print("\n7. The NaN rule that quietly drops data.")
d = pd.DataFrame({"k": ["a", "b", None, "a"], "v": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
print(f"   groupby('k').sum() ->\n{d.groupby('k')['v'].sum().to_string()}")
print(f"   the None row (v=3) was DROPPED. Total {d.groupby('k')['v'].sum().sum()} vs actual {d['v'].sum()}.")
print(f"   dropna=False keeps it ->\n{d.groupby('k', dropna=False)['v'].sum().to_string()}")

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real data lives in multiple tables. Joining customers to orders to products is bread and butter. Pandas merge mirrors SQL JOINs - inner, left, right, outer - and concat stacks DataFrames vertically or horizontally.

Concat - stacking DataFrames

import pandas as pd

# Vertical stacking (axis=0, default) - same columns
jan = pd.DataFrame({"month": "Jan", "sales": [100, 200, 300]})
feb = pd.DataFrame({"month": "Feb", "sales": [150, 250, 350]})

combined = pd.concat([jan, feb])
# Note: index has duplicates - reset if needed
combined = pd.concat([jan, feb], ignore_index=True)

# Horizontal stacking (axis=1) - same number of rows, different columns
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"b": [4, 5, 6]})
pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1)
# a b
# 0 1 4
# 1 2 5
# 2 3 6

# Many DataFrames at once - more efficient than appending one at a time
files = ["jan.csv", "feb.csv", "mar.csv"]
all_data = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f) for f in files], ignore_index=True)

Merge - SQL-style joins

customers = pd.DataFrame({
 "cust_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
 "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave"],
})

orders = pd.DataFrame({
 "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104, 105],
 "cust_id": [1, 1, 2, 3, 5],
 "amount": [100, 50, 200, 150, 300],
})

# Inner join - only matching rows (default)
pd.merge(customers, orders, on="cust_id")
# 4 rows - cust 1 (twice), 2, 3. cust 4 dropped (no orders).
# cust 5 dropped (no customer record).

# Left join - keep all customers, with NaN where no orders
pd.merge(customers, orders, on="cust_id", how="left")
# 5 rows - includes cust 4 with NaN orders

# Right join - keep all orders, NaN where no customer
pd.merge(customers, orders, on="cust_id", how="right")
# Includes the order from cust_id 5 with NaN customer name

# Full outer - keep everything
pd.merge(customers, orders, on="cust_id", how="outer")
# 6 rows - everyone, with NaNs filled in

# Method form - prefer this
customers.merge(orders, on="cust_id", how="left")

Common merge options

# Different column names in each df
left = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2], "name": ["A", "B"]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"cust_id": [1, 2], "amount": [100, 200]})

merged = left.merge(
 right,
 left_on="customer_id",
 right_on="cust_id",
 how="inner",
)

# Merge on multiple columns
df1.merge(df2, on=["region", "product"], how="left")

# Merge on index
df1.merge(df2, left_on="key", right_index=True)
df1.merge(df2, left_index=True, right_index=True)

# Suffixes for overlapping columns
df1.merge(df2, on="key", suffixes=("_left", "_right"))

# Indicator column shows which side had the row
df1.merge(df2, on="key", how="outer", indicator=True)
# Adds "_merge" column with values: left_only, right_only, both
# Useful for debugging joins
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Always check row count after a merge. 1:N joins multiply rows. N:M joins explode them. If your customer table has 10K rows and your orders have 50K, an inner join could yield anywhere from 0 to 50K rows - never 10K * 50K. validate='1:m' in merge enforces relationship type.

join() - shortcut for index-based merges

# join uses the index by default - cleaner for index-based work
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}, index=["x", "y", "z"])
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"b": [10, 20]}, index=["y", "z"])

df1.join(df2) # left join on index
df1.join(df2, how="inner")

# Equivalent merge call:
df1.merge(df2, left_index=True, right_index=True, how="left")

merge_asof - approximate matches by sort key

# Fast nearest-or-prior matching - for time series joins

trades = pd.DataFrame({
 "time": pd.to_datetime(["2024-05-01 10:00:01", "2024-05-01 10:00:05"]),
 "price": [100.5, 100.7],
})

quotes = pd.DataFrame({
 "time": pd.to_datetime(["2024-05-01 10:00:00", "2024-05-01 10:00:03",
 "2024-05-01 10:00:04"]),
 "bid": [100.4, 100.5, 100.6],
})

# For each trade, get the most recent quote BEFORE it
pd.merge_asof(trades.sort_values("time"), quotes.sort_values("time"),
 on="time")

# Within tolerance
pd.merge_asof(trades, quotes, on="time", tolerance=pd.Timedelta("2s"))

Real-world: enriching transactions

# 4 tables: orders, customers, products, regions
orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
customers = pd.read_csv("customers.csv")
products = pd.read_csv("products.csv")
regions = pd.read_csv("regions.csv")

# Join chain - each step on different keys
result = (
 orders
 .merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
 .merge(products, on="product_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
 .merge(regions, on="region_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
)

# validate="m:1" says: many orders to one customer.
# Pandas will RAISE if a customer_id appears multiple times in customers
# - catches duplicate-key bugs.

# Verify no rows lost / no rows added unexpectedly
assert len(result) == len(orders), "Row count changed!"

# Detect bad joins via indicator
debug = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", indicator=True)
debug["_merge"].value_counts()
# both: 9999 - good
# left_only: 12 - orders with no customer (DATA QUALITY BUG)

Practice

You have customers (cust_id, name, country) and orders (order_id, cust_id, amount). Compute total amount per country, including countries with zero orders.

Show solution 
import pandas as pd

# Left join customers to orders so customers with no orders are kept
merged = customers.merge(orders, on="cust_id", how="left")

# Group and sum - NaN amounts get treated as 0 by sum
country_totals = (
 merged.groupby("country", as_index=False)["amount"]
 .sum()
 .fillna(0) # in case of all-NaN groups
)

# Countries appear even if their customers had no orders

Key terms

concat
Stack DataFrames vertically (axis=0) or horizontally (axis=1).
merge
SQL-style join on shared columns or indexes.
Inner / left / right / outer
Standard SQL join types - which non-matching rows to keep.
1:1, 1:m, m:1, m:m
Cardinality of join keys; validate= catches violations.
merge_asof
Nearest-or-prior match on a sort key (e.g., timestamp joins).
indicator
Adds _merge column showing which side each row came from.

Modernization note: DataFrame.append is removed — replace with pd.concat([df, new_rows], ignore_index=True); collect pieces in a list and concat once for speed.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)

orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
                       "cust_id":  ["c1", "c2", "c9", "c1"],
                       "amount":   [100, 250, 75, 40]})
custs = pd.DataFrame({"cust_id": ["c1", "c2", "c3"],
                      "name":    ["Ann", "Bo", "Cy"],
                      "city":    ["London", "Paris", "Rome"]})
print("orders:\n" + orders.to_string(index=False))
print("\ncustomers:\n" + custs.to_string(index=False))

print("\n1. The four joins, on the same two tables.")
for how in ("inner", "left", "right", "outer"):
    m = orders.merge(custs, on="cust_id", how=how)
    print(f"\n   how='{how}'  -> {len(m)} rows, {m['name'].isna().sum()} without a customer name")
    print("   " + m.to_string(index=False).replace("\n", "\n   "))

print("\n2. Which rows did NOT match? indicator=True answers it directly.")
chk = orders.merge(custs, on="cust_id", how="outer", indicator=True)
print(chk[["order_id", "cust_id", "name", "_merge"]].to_string(index=False))
print(f"   counts: {chk['_merge'].value_counts().to_dict()}")
print("   c9 is an order for a customer who is not in the customer table; c3 is a")
print("   customer with no orders. Both are findings, not noise - check them before")
print("   you switch to an inner join and make them disappear.")

print("\n3. Duplicate keys MULTIPLY rows. This is how a total silently doubles.")
dupes = pd.DataFrame({"cust_id": ["c1", "c1", "c2"],
                      "segment": ["retail", "wholesale", "retail"]})
m = orders.merge(dupes, on="cust_id", how="left")
print(f"   orders had {len(orders)} rows; after the merge there are {len(m)}")
print("   " + m.to_string(index=False).replace("\n", "\n   "))
print(f"   sum of amount before {orders['amount'].sum()}   after {m['amount'].sum()}")
print("   c1 appears twice in the right table, so both of its orders were duplicated.")
print("   Check the key is unique BEFORE merging:")
print(f"   dupes['cust_id'].is_unique -> {dupes['cust_id'].is_unique}")
print(f"   validate='m:1' would raise instead of silently doubling:")
try:
    orders.merge(dupes, on="cust_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"   {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

print("\n4. Different column names, and overlapping ones.")
a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "value": [10, 20]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"key": [1, 2], "value": [99, 98]})
m = a.merge(b, left_on="id", right_on="key", suffixes=("_left", "_right"))
print(m.to_string(index=False))
print("   Without suffixes you would have two columns both called 'value'.")

print("\n5. concat stacks; merge joins. Do not confuse them.")
jan = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["n", "s"], "sales": [100, 200]})
feb = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["n", "s"], "sales": [110, 190]})
stacked = pd.concat([jan, feb], keys=["jan", "feb"], names=["month", "row"])
print(stacked.to_string())
print(f"   ignore_index=True instead renumbers 0..n: {list(pd.concat([jan, feb], ignore_index=True).index)}")
mismatch = pd.concat([jan, pd.DataFrame({"store": ["e"], "staff": [3]})], ignore_index=True)
print("   concat with different columns fills the gaps with NaN:")
print("   " + mismatch.to_string(index=False).replace("\n", "\n   "))

print("\n6. Joining on the index is .join(); on a column it is .merge().")
left = jan.set_index("store")
right = pd.DataFrame({"manager": ["Ann", "Bo"]}, index=["n", "s"])
print(left.join(right).to_string())

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The same data can be 'long' (one observation per row) or 'wide' (one observation per row, many measurement columns). Switching between them is fundamental for plotting, modeling, and reporting. Most beginners get stuck on this for weeks.

Long vs wide format

  • Long: each row is one observation. Columns: id, variable, value. Best for analytics, plotting libraries (seaborn, ggplot).
  • Wide: each row is one entity. Columns: id, var1, var2, var3. Best for spreadsheets, certain modeling tasks.
  • pivot: long → wide. melt: wide → long. They're inverse operations.
  • stack/unstack: do similar things but operate on the index (creating MultiIndex layers).

pivot - long to wide

import pandas as pd

# Long format
long = pd.DataFrame({
 "date": ["2024-01", "2024-01", "2024-02", "2024-02"],
 "product": ["A", "B", "A", "B"],
 "sales": [100, 200, 150, 250],
})
# date product sales
# 0 2024-01 A 100
# 1 2024-01 B 200
# 2 2024-02 A 150
# 3 2024-02 B 250

# pivot - reshape so each product becomes a column
wide = long.pivot(index="date", columns="product", values="sales")
# product A B
# date
# 2024-01 100 200
# 2024-02 150 250

# Reset index to flatten
wide = wide.reset_index()
wide.columns.name = None # remove the "product" label

# pivot fails if there are duplicate (index, columns) combinations
# Use pivot_table instead - it aggregates

pivot_table - aggregating wide format

sales = pd.DataFrame({
 "date": ["2024-01", "2024-01", "2024-01", "2024-02"],
 "region": ["East", "West", "East", "East"],
 "product": ["A", "A", "B", "A"],
 "amount": [100, 200, 50, 150],
})

# When index/columns aren't unique, pivot_table aggregates
pivoted = sales.pivot_table(
 index="date",
 columns="region",
 values="amount",
 aggfunc="sum", # default is mean
)
# region East West
# date
# 2024-01 150 200
# 2024-02 150 NaN

# Multiple aggregations
sales.pivot_table(
 index="date",
 columns="region",
 values="amount",
 aggfunc=["sum", "count", "mean"],
)

# Multiple value columns
sales.pivot_table(
 index="region",
 values=["amount", "quantity"],
 aggfunc={"amount": "sum", "quantity": "mean"},
)

# Add row/column totals
sales.pivot_table(
 index="date",
 columns="region",
 values="amount",
 aggfunc="sum",
 margins=True, # adds an "All" row and column
 margins_name="Total",
)

melt - wide to long

wide = pd.DataFrame({
 "name": ["Alice", "Bob"],
 "math": [90, 85],
 "english": [88, 92],
 "science": [95, 80],
})

# Melt - keep "name", unpivot the score columns
long = wide.melt(
 id_vars="name",
 value_vars=["math", "english", "science"],
 var_name="subject",
 value_name="score",
)
# name subject score
# 0 Alice math 90
# 1 Bob math 85
# 2 Alice english 88
# 3 Bob english 92
# 4 Alice science 95
# 5 Bob science 80

# Why melt? Many libraries expect long format:
import seaborn as sns
sns.barplot(data=long, x="subject", y="score", hue="name")

# Common pattern: read messy wide CSV, melt to long for analysis,
# then pivot back to wide for the final report

stack and unstack

Same as pivot/melt but operate on the index, producing/consuming MultiIndex.

df = pd.DataFrame({
 "math": [90, 85],
 "english": [88, 92],
}, index=["Alice", "Bob"])

# stack - move column labels into the index (wide -> long with MultiIndex)
stacked = df.stack()
# Alice math 90
# english 88
# Bob math 85
# english 92

# unstack - reverse
stacked.unstack() # back to original
stacked.unstack(level=0) # unstack the OUTER level (names)
stacked.unstack(level=-1) # default - unstack the LAST (innermost) level

# In modern pandas, .stack(future_stack=True) is recommended
stacked = df.stack(future_stack=True)

Working with MultiIndex

# Result of groupby with multiple keys is often a MultiIndex
sales = pd.DataFrame({
 "region": ["East", "East", "West", "West"],
 "year": [2023, 2024, 2023, 2024],
 "revenue": [100, 150, 200, 250],
})

result = sales.set_index(["region", "year"])
# revenue
# region year
# East 2023 100
# 2024 150
# West 2023 200
# 2024 250

# Selecting from MultiIndex
result.loc["East"] # all East rows
result.loc[("East", 2024)] # specific row
result.loc[("East", 2023):("West", 2023)] # slice

# xs - cross-section, slice across a level
result.xs(2024, level="year") # all regions for 2024

# Flatten back
result = result.reset_index()
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

After pivot_table or groupby().agg(), you often get MultiIndex columns or rows. To flatten: df.columns = ['_'.join(c).strip('_') for c in df.columns] for tuples like ('amount', 'sum') → 'amount_sum'.

Real-world: time series wide-to-long

# Survey data: one row per respondent, columns for each year
df = pd.DataFrame({
 "respondent": ["R1", "R2", "R3"],
 "score_2022": [3, 4, 5],
 "score_2023": [4, 4, 5],
 "score_2024": [5, 3, 5],
})

# Melt to long format for analysis
long = df.melt(
 id_vars="respondent",
 value_vars=["score_2022", "score_2023", "score_2024"],
 var_name="year",
 value_name="score",
)
long["year"] = long["year"].str.replace("score_", "").astype(int)

# Now we can compute year-over-year change
long = long.sort_values(["respondent", "year"])
long["yoy_change"] = long.groupby("respondent")["score"].diff()

# Or pivot summaries by year
long.pivot_table(index="year", values="score", aggfunc=["mean", "std"])

Practice

Given a wide DataFrame with columns ['name', 'q1', 'q2', 'q3', 'q4'] for quarterly sales, melt it to a long format, then pivot to a wide format showing the average per quarter across all names.

Show solution 
import pandas as pd

wide = pd.DataFrame({
 "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"],
 "q1": [100, 200, 150],
 "q2": [120, 180, 160],
 "q3": [110, 220, 170],
 "q4": [130, 210, 180],
})

# Melt
long = wide.melt(id_vars="name", var_name="quarter", value_name="sales")

# Pivot to wide with average per quarter
pivoted = long.pivot_table(values="sales", columns="quarter", aggfunc="mean")
print(pivoted)
# quarter q1 q2 q3 q4
# sales 150.00 153.3 166.7 173.3

Key terms

Long format
One observation per row; columns include id, variable, value.
Wide format
One entity per row; columns are different variables.
pivot
Long → wide; reshape value column into multiple columns by another column.
pivot_table
Like pivot but aggregates duplicate keys (configurable aggfunc).
melt
Wide → long; collapse multiple columns into id/variable/value.
MultiIndex
Hierarchical index with multiple levels - common after groupby.

Exercise calls: two-way frequency table — pd.crosstab(df.gender, df.country). One-hot encode a column — pd.get_dummies(df["category"]) — one 0/1 column per category value. In words: crosstab for gender by country counts; get_dummies to one-hot encode the category column.

Worked example

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — long and wide, and why pivot_table exists
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)

long = pd.DataFrame({
    "store":  ["north", "north", "north", "south", "south", "south"],
    "month":  ["jan", "feb", "mar", "jan", "feb", "mar"],
    "sales":  [120, 130, 125, 90, 95, 105],
    "staff":  [4, 4, 5, 3, 3, 3]})
print("LONG (tidy): one row per observation")
print(long.to_string(index=False))

print("\n1. pivot: long -> wide. One row per store, one column per month.")
wide = long.pivot(index="store", columns="month", values="sales")
print(wide.to_string())
print(f"   shape {long.shape} -> {wide.shape}; columns are now the month VALUES")

print("\n2. melt: wide -> long. The inverse.")
back = wide.reset_index().melt(id_vars="store", var_name="month", value_name="sales")
print(back.to_string(index=False))
print(f"   round-trips? {back.sort_values(['store','month']).reset_index(drop=True)['sales'].tolist() == long.sort_values(['store','month']).reset_index(drop=True)['sales'].tolist()}")

print("\n3. pivot FAILS on duplicate index/column pairs; pivot_table aggregates them.")
dup = pd.concat([long, pd.DataFrame({"store": ["north"], "month": ["jan"],
                                     "sales": [500], "staff": [9]})], ignore_index=True)
try:
    dup.pivot(index="store", columns="month", values="sales")
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"   pivot -> ValueError: {str(e)[:70]}")
pt = dup.pivot_table(index="store", columns="month", values="sales", aggfunc="sum")
print("   pivot_table(aggfunc='sum') handles it:")
print(pt.to_string())
print("   That is the real difference: pivot reshapes, pivot_table reshapes AND aggregates.")

print("\n4. pivot_table with margins gives you the totals row and column.")
pt2 = long.pivot_table(index="store", columns="month", values="sales",
                       aggfunc="sum", margins=True, margins_name="TOTAL")
print(pt2.to_string())

print("\n5. stack and unstack move a level between rows and columns.")
st = wide.stack()
print(f"   wide.stack() -> a Series with a MultiIndex {st.index.names}:")
print(st.to_string())
print(f"   .unstack() puts it back: shape {st.unstack().shape}")
print(f"   unstack(0) pivots the OTHER level instead:\n{st.unstack(0).to_string()}")

print("\n6. Multiple value columns at once.")
mv = long.pivot(index="store", columns="month", values=["sales", "staff"])
print(mv.to_string())
print(f"   columns are a MultiIndex: {list(mv.columns)[:3]}...")
print(f"   flattened: {['_'.join(map(str, c)) for c in mv.columns]}")

print("\n7. Which shape do you want?")
for use, shape in [("storing and appending records", "LONG"),
                   ("groupby, merge, most pandas work", "LONG"),
                   ("a table a human reads", "WIDE"),
                   ("most plotting libraries", "LONG"),
                   ("a correlation matrix / heatmap", "WIDE")]:
    print(f"   {use:34} {shape}")
print("   Keep data long while you work on it; reshape to wide only at the moment you")
print("   present it.")

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Time-aware data is everywhere - sales, clicks, sensor readings. Pandas datetime is rich and fast. Knowing how to parse, slice, resample, and compute deltas saves you from the swamp of string manipulation.

Parsing dates

import pandas as pd

# When reading CSV
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_date", "ship_date"])

# After loading
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])

# Custom format - much faster than auto-detect for big files
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")

# Common formats - cheat sheet

Time zones are sneaky. pd.to_datetime creates naive timestamps by default. Use tz_localize('UTC') to mark a timezone, then tz_convert('US/Eastern') to view in another. Mixing naive and aware timestamps in operations raises errors.

Real-world: cohort retention

# orders: customer_id, order_date
orders["order_month"] = orders["order_date"].dt.to_period("M")

# Each customer's first order month = their cohort
orders["cohort"] = orders.groupby("customer_id")["order_month"].transform("min")

# Periods since cohort
orders["months_since_signup"] = (
 (orders["order_month"] - orders["cohort"]).apply(lambda x: x.n)
)

# Retention table: cohort vs months_since
retention = orders.pivot_table(
 index="cohort",
 columns="months_since_signup",
 values="customer_id",
 aggfunc="nunique",
)

# Convert to retention rates
retention_pct = retention.div(retention.iloc[:, 0], axis=0)

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)

print("1. Parse once, then everything else is easy.")
raw = pd.DataFrame({"when": ["2024-01-05 09:30", "2024-01-05 14:00", "2024-02-11 08:15",
                             "2024-02-29 23:59", "2024-03-02 12:00"],
                    "amount": [100, 250, 75, 40, 310]})
print(f"   before: {raw['when'].dtype}")
raw["when"] = pd.to_datetime(raw["when"])
print(f"   after : {raw['when'].dtype}")
print(raw.to_string(index=False))

print("\n2. The .dt accessor exposes every component.")
d = raw["when"].dt
comp = pd.DataFrame({"year": d.year, "month": d.month, "day": d.day,
                     "hour": d.hour, "dayofweek": d.dayofweek,
                     "day_name": d.day_name(), "quarter": d.quarter,
                     "is_month_end": d.is_month_end})
print(comp.to_string(index=False))
print("   dayofweek is 0=Monday. 2024-02-29 is_month_end is True - 2024 is a leap year,")
print("   which is exactly the case a hand-written date parser gets wrong.")

print("\n3. Timedeltas are real objects, not just numbers.")
gap = raw["when"].max() - raw["when"].min()
print(f"   span: {gap}   -> {gap.days} days, {gap.total_seconds():,.0f} seconds")
raw["since_first"] = raw["when"] - raw["when"].min()
print(f"   days since the first order: {raw['since_first'].dt.days.tolist()}")
print(f"   add a period: {raw['when'].iloc[0]} + 45 days = {raw['when'].iloc[0] + pd.Timedelta(days=45)}")
print(f"   month-aware offset: + 1 month = {raw['when'].iloc[0] + pd.DateOffset(months=1)}")

print("\n4. A DatetimeIndex unlocks resampling and partial-string slicing.")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=90, freq="D")
ts = pd.Series(100 + np.arange(90) * 0.5 + rng.normal(0, 5, 90).round(2), index=idx, name="value")
print(f"   series of {len(ts)} daily points from {ts.index.min().date()} to {ts.index.max().date()}")
print(f"   ts['2024-02'] selects a whole month: {len(ts['2024-02'])} rows")
print(f"   ts['2024-01-10':'2024-01-13'] -> {ts['2024-01-10':'2024-01-13'].round(1).tolist()}")

print("\n5. resample is groupby for time.")
monthly = ts.resample("ME").agg(["count", "mean", "max"]).round(2)
print(monthly.to_string())
print(f"   weekly mean, first 4: {ts.resample('W').mean().round(2).head(4).tolist()}")
print("   Upsampling creates gaps you must decide how to fill:")
hourly = ts.head(3).resample("12h").asfreq()
print(f"   asfreq() leaves NaN: {hourly.round(1).tolist()}")
print(f"   ffill() carries the last value: {ts.head(3).resample('12h').ffill().round(1).tolist()}")

print("\n6. Rolling windows: the moving average, done right.")
roll = pd.DataFrame({"value": ts, "ma7": ts.rolling(7).mean().round(2),
                     "ma7_min": ts.rolling(7, min_periods=1).mean().round(2)})
print(roll.head(8).to_string())
print("   The first 6 rows of ma7 are NaN because a 7-day window is not full yet. That")
print("   is correct: min_periods=1 fills them, but those early values average fewer")
print("   days and are not comparable with the rest.")

print("\n7. Naive vs aware, again - it bites here too.")
naive = pd.Timestamp("2024-06-01 12:00")
utc = naive.tz_localize("UTC")
ny = utc.tz_convert("America/New_York")
print(f"   naive        {naive}  tz={naive.tz}")
print(f"   tz_localize  {utc}")
print(f"   tz_convert   {ny}")
print("   tz_localize ATTACHES a zone (the clock reading does not change).")
print("   tz_convert MOVES to another zone (the clock reading does change).")
try:
    naive - utc
except TypeError as e:
    print(f"   mixing them: TypeError: {str(e)[:64]}")

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Method chaining lets you express a whole transformation pipeline as one readable expression - no intermediate variables, no df reassignments. Combined with .pipe() for custom functions, it's the most maintainable pandas style.

The chaining style

# Old style - many intermediate variables
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
df = df.dropna(subset=["amount"])
df = df[df["status"] == "shipped"]
df["amount_usd"] = df["amount"] * df["fx_rate"]
df = df.groupby("region").agg(total=("amount_usd", "sum"))
df = df.sort_values("total", ascending=False)
result = df.head(10)

# Chained style - one expression, top-down read
result = (
 pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
 .dropna(subset=["amount"])
 .query("status == 'shipped'")
 .assign(amount_usd=lambda d: d["amount"] * d["fx_rate"])
 .groupby("region", as_index=False)
 .agg(total=("amount_usd", "sum"))
 .sort_values("total", ascending=False)
 .head(10)
)

# Wrap the whole expression in parentheses to allow line breaks

assign() - add columns inline

# Without assign - breaks the chain
df["new_col"] = df["x"] * 2
result = df.groupby("group").mean()

# With assign - keeps the chain going
result = (
 df
 .assign(new_col=lambda d: d["x"] * 2)
 .groupby("group")
 .mean()
)

# Multiple new columns at once
result = df.assign(
 profit=lambda d: d["revenue"] - d["cost"],
 margin=lambda d: (d["revenue"] - d["cost"]) / d["revenue"],
 log_revenue=lambda d: np.log1p(d["revenue"]),
)

# Why lambda d: d["x"] * 2 instead of df["x"] * 2 ?
# - Lambda refers to the CURRENT state of the chain
# - df["x"] uses the original df (before any chain transformations)

# Subtle bug:
df.dropna().assign(scaled=df["x"] / df["x"].max()) # uses ORIGINAL df["x"]
df.dropna().assign(scaled=lambda d: d["x"] / d["x"].max()) # uses dropped df

pipe() - inject custom functions

# pipe lets you put your own functions into a chain

def remove_outliers(df, col, n_std=3):
 """Remove rows where col is > n_std away from mean."""
 mean = df[col].mean()
 std = df[col].std()
 return df[(df[col] - mean).abs() < n_std * std]

result = (
 df
 .dropna()
 .pipe(remove_outliers, col="amount", n_std=3)
 .query("status == 'shipped'")
 .groupby("region")
 .agg(total=("amount", "sum"))
)

# Without pipe, you'd have to break the chain:
clean = df.dropna()
clean = remove_outliers(clean, col="amount", n_std=3)
clean = clean.query(...)
# pipe keeps it readable

# Pipe is also great for unit-testable transformations
def calculate_metrics(df):
 return df.assign(
 margin=lambda d: (d["revenue"] - d["cost"]) / d["revenue"],
 is_profitable=lambda d: d["margin"] > 0.1,
 )

# Now you can:
df.pipe(calculate_metrics)
# AND test calculate_metrics independently with pytest

Common chain patterns

# Top N per group
top_3_per_region = (
 df
 .sort_values(["region", "amount"], ascending=[True, False])
 .groupby("region")
 .head(3)
)

# Compute metrics by group
group_summary = (
 df
 .groupby("category", as_index=False)
 .agg(
 n_items=("id", "count"),
 avg_price=("price", "mean"),
 max_price=("price", "max"),
 )
 .sort_values("n_items", ascending=False)
)

# Filter then transform

 events

 .groupby("user_id", as_index=False)
 .agg(events=("event_date", "count"))

)

# Join then aggregate
revenue_per_country = (
 orders
 .merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")
 .merge(countries, on="country_code", how="left")
 .groupby("country_name", as_index=False)
 ["amount"].sum()

)

Long chains can be hard to debug because you can't easily inspect intermediate state. When debugging, break the chain at the suspect step and inspect, OR use .pipe(lambda d: (print(d.shape), d)[1]) to log without breaking. Once it works, recombine.

Debugging chains

# Insert pipe steps to log
def log(df, label):
 print(f"{label}: shape={df.shape}, cols={list(df.columns)}")
 return df

result = (
 df
 .pipe(log, "after load")
 .dropna()
 .pipe(log, "after dropna")
 .query("amount > 0")
 .pipe(log, "after filter")
 .groupby("region").sum()
 .pipe(log, "after group")
)

# Or use a helper class for breakpoints in chains
def inspect(df):
 print(df.head())
 print(df.dtypes)
 print(df.shape)
 return df

result = df.pipe(inspect).dropna().pipe(inspect)

When NOT to chain

# Don't chain when you need the intermediate results
# Bad - can't easily reuse the cleaned df
report = (
 pd.read_csv("data.csv").dropna()
 .pipe(my_transform)
 .groupby("x").mean()
 .to_csv("report.csv")
)

# Better when you need the cleaned df elsewhere
clean = pd.read_csv("data.csv").dropna().pipe(my_transform)
clean.to_csv("clean.csv")

report = clean.groupby("x").mean()
report.to_csv("report.csv")

# Rule of thumb: if you'd reference the intermediate value more than once,
# break the chain. If it's a pure one-shot transformation, chain it.

Key terms

Method chaining
Calling multiple methods sequentially in one expression.
assign()

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
raw = pd.DataFrame({

    "region": ["N", "S", "E", "W", "N", "N", "S", "E"],
    "sales":  [120, 90, 140, 200, 75, 130, 95, 145],
    "staff":  [4, 3, 5, 7, 2, 4, 3, 5],
    "status": ["open", "open", "closed", "open", "open", "open", "closed", "open"]})
print(raw.to_string(index=False))

print("\n1. The same job written twice. First, the way it usually starts.")
df = raw.copy()
df = df[df["status"] == "open"]

df = df[df["per_staff"] > 25]

result_a = df.groupby("region")["sales"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f"   {len(result_a)} regions: {result_a.to_dict()}")
print("   Five statements, one name reused five times. Run cell 3 twice and 'df' is")
print("   no longer what the next line assumes - the notebook bug from chapter 3.")

print("\n2. The same thing as one expression.")
result_b = (raw
            .query("status == 'open'")
            .assign(per_staff=lambda d: d["sales"] / d["staff"],
                    band=lambda d: np.where(d["sales"] >= 130, "high", "low"))
            .query("per_staff > 25")
            .groupby("region")["sales"].sum()
            .sort_values(ascending=False))
print(f"   {len(result_b)} regions: {result_b.to_dict()}")
print(f"   identical to the step-by-step version? {result_a.equals(result_b)}")
print(f"   the original is untouched: {list(raw.columns)}")

print("\n3. lambda inside assign is what makes it work.")
print("   assign(x=d['a']) would use the frame as it was BEFORE the chain started.")
print("   assign(x=lambda d: d['a']) sees the frame at THAT point in the chain:")
demo = (raw
        .assign(per_staff=lambda d: (d["sales"] / d["staff"]).round(1))
        .assign(rank=lambda d: d["per_staff"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)))
print(demo[["store", "sales", "staff", "per_staff", "rank"]].head(4).to_string(index=False))
print("   The second assign depends on the column the first one created.")

print("\n4. pipe drops your own function into the chain.")
def drop_small(d, floor):
    return d[d["sales"] >= floor]
def add_share(d):
    return d.assign(share=(d["sales"] / d["sales"].sum() * 100).round(1))
out = (raw
       .query("status == 'open'")
       .pipe(drop_small, floor=100)
       .pipe(add_share)
       .loc[:, ["store", "sales", "share"]])
print(out.to_string(index=False))
print("   pipe(f, args) is just f(df, args) - but it keeps the chain readable, and each")
print("   function stays small enough to unit-test on its own.")

print("\n5. Debugging a chain without breaking it up.")
def peek(d, label):
    print(f"      [{label}] {d.shape}  columns={list(d.columns)}")
    return d
_ = (raw
     .pipe(peek, "start")
     .query("status == 'open'").pipe(peek, "after filter")
     .assign(per_staff=lambda d: d["sales"] / d["staff"]).pipe(peek, "after assign")
     .groupby("region")["sales"].sum())
print("   A pass-through function that prints and returns the frame unchanged lets you")
print("   watch the shape at every step - the usual objection to chaining, answered.")

print("\n6. When NOT to chain.")
for rule in ["a chain longer than about 8 steps - split it into named functions",
             "anything you need to reuse - that is a function, not a chain",
             "expensive intermediates you want to keep - assign them a name",
             "a step you cannot read aloud in one breath"]:

[start] (8, 5) columns=['store', 'region', 'sales', 'staff', 'status'] [after filter] (6, 5) columns=['store', 'region', 'sales', 'staff', 'status'] [after assign] (6, 6) columns=['store', 'region', 'sales', 'staff', 'status', 'per_staff'] A pass-through function that prints and returns the frame unchanged lets you watch the shape at every step - the usual objection to chaining, answered. 6. When NOT to chain. - a chain longer than about 8 steps - split it into named functions - anything you need to reuse - that is a function, not a chain - expensive intermediates you want to keep - assign them a name - a step you cannot read aloud in one breath
actual output, captured from Python 3.11

Walk through it: the step-by-step version rebinds one name five times, and the chained version is a single expression producing an identical result - verified with .equals(), not claimed. The argument for chaining is not aesthetics: reusing df five times means running cell 3 twice leaves it in a state the next line does not expect, which is the notebook bug from chapter 3 in a different costume. Section 3 explains the piece that makes it work - assign(x=lambda d: ...) sees the frame at that point in the chain, so the second assign can use the column the first one created. Section 4 shows pipe dropping your own functions in, which keeps each one small enough to unit-test. Section 5 answers the usual objection with a pass-through peek function that prints the shape at every step without breaking the chain. Section 6 says when not to chain.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the first thing you do with any new dataset and the last thing you skip when things go wrong. It catches data quality issues, suggests feature engineering, surfaces relationships, and tells you whether your modeling assumptions are reasonable. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests systematic exploration workflow, summary statistics, and visual diagnostics.

The EDA workflow

★ STANDARD EDA STEPS
  1. Load and inspect shape: rows, columns, dtypes
  2. Summary statistics: mean, median, ranges, missing rates
  3. Univariate: distribution of each feature
  4. Bivariate: relationships between features (correlations, scatter plots)
  5. Target analysis: distribution + feature-target relationships
  6. Quality checks: outliers, duplicates, leakage suspects
  7. Document findings: list issues to fix before modeling

Step 1: load and inspect

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('customers.csv')

# Shape
print(f"Rows: {len(df):,}, Cols: {df.shape[1]}")

# Sample
df.head() # first 5 rows
df.tail() # last 5
df.sample(10) # random 10

# Schema
df.info()
# Column names, dtypes, non-null counts, memory usage

# Memory check (especially for big data)
df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1024**2 # MB

# Inspect column types
df.dtypes.value_counts()
# int64 12
# float64 8
# object 5
# datetime64 2

Step 2: summary statistics

# Numeric summary
df.describe()
# Returns count, mean, std, min, 25%, 50%, 75%, max for numeric cols

# Categorical summary
df.describe(include='object')
# count, unique, top, freq

# All columns
df.describe(include='all')

# Per-column quick check
df['age'].describe()
df['age'].value_counts()
df['age'].nunique()
df['age'].quantile([0.01, 0.05, 0.5, 0.95, 0.99]) # see tails

# Find suspicious values
df['age'].min(), df['age'].max()
# age = -1 or age = 999 → likely sentinel for missing

Step 3: missing values

# Counts per column
df.isna().sum().sort_values(ascending=False)

# Rates (often more useful)
(df.isna().mean() * 100).round(1).sort_values(ascending=False)

# Total cells
df.isna().sum().sum()

# Rows with ANY missing
df.isna().any(axis=1).sum()

# Pattern visualization
import seaborn as sns
sns.heatmap(df.isna(), cbar=False, yticklabels=False)
# Reveals patterns — block of missing rows? Column-wide gaps?

# Optional library: missingno
# import missingno as msno
# msno.matrix(df) # missing-value matrix
# msno.bar(df) # bar of non-null counts
# msno.heatmap(df) # correlation of missingness

Step 4: univariate analysis

Numeric distributions

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Histogram for each numeric column
df.select_dtypes(include='number').hist(bins=30, figsize=(15, 10))
plt.tight_layout()

# Box plot for outlier detection
df.select_dtypes(include='number').boxplot(figsize=(12, 6), rot=45)

# KDE for smooth distribution
sns.kdeplot(data=df['income'])

# Things to look for:
# - Skewness (right tail → log transform candidate)
# - Bimodality (two peaks → maybe a categorical hiding inside)
# - Outliers (whiskers, isolated points)
# - Unrealistic values (negative ages, future dates)

Categorical distributions

# Bar chart of value counts
df['city'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar')

# Top N + "Other" for high cardinality
top = df['product_category'].value_counts().head(10)
other = df['product_category'].value_counts().iloc[10:].sum()
combined = pd.concat([top, pd.Series([other], index=['Other'])])
combined.plot(kind='barh')

# Cardinality check
for col in df.select_dtypes(include='object'):
 print(f"{col}: {df[col].nunique()} unique values")
# Very-high-cardinality categorical = consider target encoding or hashing

Step 5: bivariate analysis

Numeric-numeric: correlation

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

corr = df.select_dtypes(include='number').corr()
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, cmap='RdBu_r', center=0, fmt='.2f')

# Pairs with |r| > 0.95 likely redundant — pick one
# Pair with target = candidate predictor

# Scatter plot for two specific features
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='income', y='spend', alpha=0.5)

# Pairplot for all combinations (use on small subsets — slow)
sns.pairplot(df[['age', 'income', 'tenure', 'target']],
 hue='target',
 diag_kind='kde')

Categorical-numeric: group statistics

df.groupby('city')['income'].describe()

# Box plot per group
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='city', y='income')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)

# Violin plot — distribution per group
sns.violinplot(data=df, x='product_tier', y='order_value')

Categorical-categorical: cross-tabs

pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier'])
pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier'], normalize='index') # row proportions

# Heatmap visualization
sns.heatmap(pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier']), annot=True, fmt='d')

Step 6: target analysis

# Classification: class balance
df['churned'].value_counts(normalize=True)
# 0 0.85
# 1 0.15
# → imbalanced — plan accordingly

# Regression: target distribution
sns.histplot(df['price'], bins=50, kde=True)
# Right-skewed → consider log transform

# Target vs each feature (numeric)
for col in numeric_features:
 sns.boxplot(data=df, x='target', y=col)
 plt.show()

# Target vs each feature (categorical)
for col in categorical_features:
 sns.barplot(data=df, x=col, y='target') # avg target per category
 plt.xticks(rotation=45)
 plt.show()

Step 7: quality checks

# Duplicates
df.duplicated().sum()
df[df.duplicated(keep=False)].sort_values(list(df.columns)) # see them

# Drop duplicates
df = df.drop_duplicates()

# Or partial duplicates (same primary key)
df.duplicated(subset=['customer_id', 'order_date']).sum()

# Outlier detection (IQR rule)
def find_outliers(s):
 q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
 iqr = q3 - q1
 return s[(s < q1 - 1.5*iqr) | (s > q3 + 1.5*iqr)]

find_outliers(df['income'])

# Constant or near-constant features (low variance → useless)
for col in df.select_dtypes(include='number'):
 if df[col].nunique() < 5:
 print(f"{col}: only {df[col].nunique()} unique values")

# Data leakage suspects:
# - Features computed AFTER the target was known
# - Features that are too good (correlation > 0.95 with target)
# - Identifier columns that uniquely determine the target

Pandas profiling — automated EDA

# Quick-and-dirty automated report
# pip install ydata-profiling
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Data Profile", explorative=True)
profile.to_file("eda_report.html")

# Generates a full HTML report:
# - Summary stats per column
# - Distributions
# - Correlations
# - Missing values matrix
# - Common warnings (high cardinality, skewed, etc.)

# Faster alternatives: sweetviz, dtale, ydata-profiling
# Good first pass; don't replace manual EDA

EDA checklist for any new dataset

★ THE 12-POINT CHECKLIST
  1. Shape and dtypes (df.info())
  2. First/last few rows + random sample
  3. Numeric describe()
  4. Categorical describe(include='object')
  5. Missing-value counts and rates
  6. Cardinality of each column
  7. Histograms / boxplots for numeric features
  8. Value-counts for categorical features
  9. Correlation matrix among numerics
  10. Target distribution (class balance or skew)
  11. Feature-target relationships (univariate)
  12. Duplicates, outliers, leakage suspects

Common EDA mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Skipping EDA and going straight to modeling — catches every bug too late
  2. Treating describe() as enough — always plot too
  3. Not checking for sentinel values — -999, "NA" hide as valid data
  4. Ignoring class imbalance — model can be 99% accurate trivially
  5. Forgetting to look at TARGET vs features — finds the strong predictors
  6. Plotting everything raw without log transform — skewed features hide patterns
  7. Not checking duplicates — they inflate model "confidence"
  8. Pairplots on huge datasets — slow; sample first
  9. Trusting automated profilers blindly — they miss domain-specific issues
  10. Doing EDA on the TEST set — leakage; do it on training only
★ ON THE EXAM

"df.info()?" → Schema: column names, dtypes, non-null counts.

"df.describe()?" → Numeric summary (count, mean, std, min, 25%, 50%, 75%, max).

"df.describe(include='all')?" → Includes categorical and numeric.

"Missing rates?" → df.isna().mean().

"Duplicate rows?" → df.duplicated().sum().

"Correlation matrix?" → df.corr(); plot with sns.heatmap.

"Value counts?" → df['col'].value_counts().

"Class imbalance?" → df['target'].value_counts(normalize=True).

"Outlier detection?" → IQR rule (Q1 - 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR) or boxplot.

"Distribution shape?" → Histogram + KDE.

"Sentinel values?" → -999, "NA", "?", empty strings; convert to NaN first.

"Automated EDA tool?" → ydata-profiling, sweetviz, dtale.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • EDA is the first step on every dataset and a lifesaver when modeling goes wrong
  • Standard flow: shape → summary stats → univariate → bivariate → target analysis → quality checks
  • df.info(), df.describe(), df.head() are the first three commands on every dataset
  • Always check missing values: counts AND rates per column
  • Watch for sentinel values (-999, "NA") — convert to NaN before treating as missing
  • Histograms + boxplots reveal skew, outliers, and unrealistic values
  • Correlation matrix is the workhorse of bivariate numeric analysis
  • For high-cardinality categoricals, plot top 10 + "Other"
  • Target analysis: class balance for classification; skew for regression
  • Feature-target plots highlight strong predictors before modeling
  • Check duplicates, outliers, and leakage suspects before splitting data
  • Automated profilers (ydata-profiling) give a first-pass report — don't replace manual review
  • Do EDA only on TRAINING data — touching test data biases your modeling choices
  • Document findings: list issues to fix, decisions made, and reasoning

Worked example

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the eight checks to run before forming any opinion
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 500
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer": [f"c{i%420}" for i in range(n)],                 # deliberate duplicates
    "age":      rng.integers(18, 80, n).astype(float),
    "income":   rng.lognormal(10.5, 0.5, n).round(0),
    "spend":    rng.gamma(2, 300, n).round(2),
    "region":   rng.choice(["N", "S", "E", "W"], n, p=[.4, .3, .2, .1]),
    "signup":   pd.to_datetime("2023-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, 700, n), "D")})
df.loc[rng.choice(n, 45, replace=False), "age"] = np.nan
df.loc[rng.choice(n, 12, replace=False), "income"] = np.nan
df.loc[rng.choice(n, 3, replace=False), "spend"] *= 25            # planted outliers
df.loc[5, "age"] = 214                                            # impossible value

print("1. Shape and dtypes. Before anything else.")
print(f"   {df.shape[0]} rows x {df.shape[1]} columns")
print(df.dtypes.to_string())
print(f"   memory {df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.2f} MB")

print("\n2. Missing values, as a count AND a share.")
miss = pd.DataFrame({"missing": df.isna().sum(),
                     "pct": (df.isna().mean() * 100).round(1)})
print(miss[miss["missing"] > 0].to_string())
print(f"   complete rows: {(~df.isna().any(axis=1)).sum()} of {len(df)}")
print("   9% of age missing is a decision to make, not a row to drop reflexively -")
print("   dropping every incomplete row here would cost you 11% of the data.")

print("\n3. Duplicates - on the whole row, and on the key that should be unique.")
print(f"   fully duplicated rows      {df.duplicated().sum()}")
print(f"   duplicated 'customer' ids  {df['customer'].duplicated().sum()}")
print(f"   distinct customers         {df['customer'].nunique()} for {len(df)} rows")
print("   That is not necessarily wrong - it may be one row per ORDER. But you have to")
print("   know which, because every per-customer average depends on it.")

print("\n4. Distributions - and the reason to read the percentiles, not just the mean.")
print(df[["age", "income", "spend"]].describe(percentiles=[.01, .25, .5, .75, .99]).round(1).to_string())
print(f"   spend: mean {df['spend'].mean():.0f} vs median {df['spend'].median():.0f}")
print(f"   skew {df['spend'].skew():.2f} - a long right tail pulls the mean above the median.")
print("   For skewed money data the median is the honest 'typical' value.")

print("\n5. Impossible values hide inside a plausible range.")
print(f"   age min {df['age'].min():.0f}  max {df['age'].max():.0f}")
bad = df[(df["age"] < 18) | (df["age"] > 110)]
print(f"   ages outside 18-110: {len(bad)} row(s) -> {bad['age'].tolist()}")
print("   A range check on what the column MEANS catches what describe() shows but does")
print("   not flag. 214 sat quietly inside 'max'.")

print("\n6. Outliers: define them before you look, then count them.")
for col in ("spend", "income"):
    s = df[col].dropna()
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75]); iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    z = ((s - s.mean()) / s.std()).abs()
    print(f"   {col:7} IQR fence [{lo:,.0f}, {hi:,.0f}] -> {((s < lo) | (s > hi)).sum():>3} flagged"
          f"   |z|>3 -> {(z > 3).sum():>3} flagged")
print("   The two rules disagree because z-scores use the mean and sd, which the outliers")
print("   themselves inflate. On skewed data prefer the IQR fence.")

print("\n7. Categorical balance, before you model or split anything.")
vc = df["region"].value_counts()
print(pd.DataFrame({"count": vc, "pct": (vc / len(df) * 100).round(1)}).to_string())
print(f"   rarest class has {vc.min()} rows - too few to trust a per-region estimate,")
print("   and too few to survive a random train/test split intact.")

print("\n8. Only now: relationships.")
print(df[["age", "income", "spend"]].corr().round(3).to_string())
print("   Correlation is linear-only and outlier-sensitive. Compare with Spearman, which")
print("   ranks instead of measuring distance:")
print(df[["age", "income", "spend"]].corr(method="spearman").round(3).to_string())
print("   A big gap between the two is a signal: either a non-linear relationship, or")
print("   outliers driving the Pearson number.")
