📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Univariate analysis examines one variable at a time. It tells you the shape, central tendency, spread, and oddities of each column — and what feature engineering or modeling decisions follow. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests distribution diagnostics, skewness/kurtosis, and tests for normality.

Numeric variables — central tendency and spread

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

s = df['income']

# Central tendency
s.mean()
s.median() # robust to outliers; preferred for skewed data
s.mode() # most common value(s)

# Spread
s.std() # sample SD
s.var() # variance
s.min(), s.max()
s.max() - s.min() # range
s.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
iqr = s.quantile(0.75) - s.quantile(0.25)
s.mad() # mean absolute deviation (deprecated in newer pandas — use stats.median_abs_deviation)

# Coefficient of variation — scale-free
cv = s.std() / s.mean()

# Robust SD via MAD (median absolute deviation)
from scipy.stats import median_abs_deviation
mad = median_abs_deviation(s, scale='normal') # equivalent to SD for normal data

Shape — skewness and kurtosis

SKEWNESS AND KURTOSIS
Skewness: asymmetry of the distribution.
  0 = symmetric; positive = right tail; negative = left tail
  |skew| > 1 = highly skewed; consider log transform

Kurtosis: tailedness.
  0 (excess kurtosis) = normal; positive = heavy tails; negative = light tails
  Pandas uses "excess kurtosis" (normal = 0); some libraries use raw (normal = 3) 
s.skew() # 0 = symmetric
s.kurtosis() # 0 = normal (excess kurtosis)

# Examples:
# Income (right-skewed): skew ≈ +2
# Test scores (left-skewed): skew ≈ -1.5
# Normal distribution: skew ≈ 0, kurt ≈ 0
# Heavy-tailed (returns): kurt > 3 (highly leptokurtic)

# Rough thresholds:
# |skew| < 0.5: roughly symmetric
# 0.5 < |skew| < 1.0: moderately skewed
# |skew| > 1: highly skewed (transform candidate)

Visualizing distributions

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Histogram with KDE
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
sns.histplot(s, bins=30, kde=True, ax=ax)

# Box plot — see outliers
sns.boxplot(x=s)

# Violin — distribution shape + outliers
sns.violinplot(x=s)

# Q-Q plot — diagnose normality
from scipy import stats
stats.probplot(s.dropna(), dist='norm', plot=plt)
# Points on the line → normal
# S-curve → heavy or light tails
# Curve → skewed

# All four together for one variable
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
sns.histplot(s, bins=30, kde=True, ax=axes[0, 0]); axes[0, 0].set_title('Histogram')
sns.boxplot(x=s, ax=axes[0, 1]); axes[0, 1].set_title('Box')
sns.violinplot(x=s, ax=axes[1, 0]); axes[1, 0].set_title('Violin')
stats.probplot(s.dropna(), dist='norm', plot=axes[1, 1]); axes[1, 1].set_title('Q-Q')

Normality tests

from scipy import stats

# Shapiro-Wilk — best for small samples (n < 5000)
stat, p = stats.shapiro(s.dropna())
# H₀: data is normal
# p < 0.05 → reject normality

# Kolmogorov-Smirnov — comparing to any distribution
stat, p = stats.kstest(s.dropna(), 'norm', args=(s.mean(), s.std()))

# D'Agostino's K² — based on skewness and kurtosis; works for larger n
stat, p = stats.normaltest(s.dropna())

# Anderson-Darling — sensitive to tails
result = stats.anderson(s.dropna(), dist='norm')

# With large samples, normality tests REJECT for trivial deviations
# Use Q-Q plot as visual guide; tests as confirmation
# Most ML doesn't need normal features — CLT handles aggregates

Categorical variables — value counts and entropy

cat = df['product_category']

# Frequency
cat.value_counts()
cat.value_counts(normalize=True) # proportions
cat.value_counts(dropna=False) # include NaN counts

# Cardinality
cat.nunique()
cat.nunique() / len(df) # fraction unique (1.0 = ID column)

# Top N + others
top_n = cat.value_counts().head(10)

# Entropy — concentration / diversity
from scipy.stats import entropy
ent = entropy(cat.value_counts(normalize=True))
# Higher entropy = more uniform distribution
# Lower entropy = a few categories dominate
# Maximum entropy = log(k) where k = number of categories

Visualizing categorical distributions

import seaborn as sns

# Bar chart
sns.countplot(data=df, x='city', order=df['city'].value_counts().index)
plt.xticks(rotation=45)

# Horizontal bar — better when many categories
df['city'].value_counts().head(20).plot(kind='barh')

# Pie chart — ONLY for < 5 categories
df['city'].value_counts().plot(kind='pie', autopct='%1.1f%%')
# Pie charts are usually inferior to bar charts; consider before using

# Top N + other
top = df['city'].value_counts().head(10)
other = df['city'].value_counts().iloc[10:].sum()
combined = pd.concat([top, pd.Series([other], index=['Other'])])
combined.plot(kind='bar')

Date / time univariate

import pandas as pd

dates = pd.to_datetime(df['order_date'])

# Range
print(f"Start: {dates.min()}")
print(f"End: {dates.max()}")
print(f"Span: {dates.max() - dates.min()}")

# Frequency by year, month, etc.
dates.dt.year.value_counts().sort_index()
dates.dt.dayofweek.value_counts().sort_index() # 0=Mon, 6=Sun
dates.dt.month.value_counts().sort_index()
dates.dt.hour.value_counts().sort_index()

# Time series of daily counts
dates.dt.date.value_counts().sort_index().plot()

# Detect gaps in date ranges
all_dates = pd.date_range(dates.min(), dates.max(), freq='D')
missing_dates = all_dates.difference(dates.dt.normalize().unique())
print(f"Missing dates: {len(missing_dates)}")

Diagnostic table — one row per column

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def univariate_summary(df):
 """One row per column with diagnostic stats."""
 rows = []
 for col in df.columns:
 s = df[col]
 info = {
 'column': col,
 'dtype': s.dtype,
 'count': s.count(),
 'missing': s.isna().sum(),
 'missing_pct': s.isna().mean() * 100,
 'unique': s.nunique(),
 }
 if s.dtype.kind in 'biufc': # numeric
 info.update({
 'min': s.min(), 'max': s.max(),
 'mean': s.mean(), 'median': s.median(),
 'std': s.std(),
 'skew': s.skew(),
 'kurtosis': s.kurtosis()
 })
 rows.append(info)
 return pd.DataFrame(rows)

summary = univariate_summary(df)
print(summary)
# Quick scan for: high missing, low cardinality, extreme skew/kurtosis

Decisions that follow from univariate analysis

ObservationLikely action
High skew (|skew| > 1)Log or Box-Cox transform
Heavy tails (high kurtosis)Robust scaling; consider winsorizing
Many unique values for low-cardinality intended columnClean/normalize categorical inconsistencies
High cardinality (1000+ categories)Target encoding, hashing, or drop
Bimodal histogramCheck if a categorical is hidden inside
Most values are zeroConsider sparse representation or zero-inflated model
Constant or near-constantDrop (no predictive value)
Q-Q plot far from lineTransform or use non-parametric methods

Common univariate mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Trusting mean on skewed data — median is more representative
  2. Reporting std for non-normal data without context — IQR or MAD is better
  3. Relying on normality tests for big data — they reject trivially
  4. Skipping the Q-Q plot — most informative single diagnostic
  5. Plotting only the histogram — boxplot reveals outliers more clearly
  6. Pie charts for many categories — bar charts almost always better
  7. Forgetting to check date ranges — missing dates / future dates are common bugs
  8. Confusing kurtosis with skewness — kurtosis is tailedness, not asymmetry
  9. Using nunique() == 1 as the only "useless" check — also flag near-constant columns (e.g., 99% one value)
  10. Ignoring NaN in value_counts — default excludes; use dropna=False
★ ON THE EXAM

"Central tendency for skewed data?" → Median, not mean.

"Robust spread measure?" → IQR or MAD.

"Pandas skewness?" → s.skew(); 0 = symmetric.

"Pandas kurtosis?" → s.kurtosis(); 0 = normal (excess kurtosis).

"|skew| > 1?" → Highly skewed; consider log transform.

"Q-Q plot?" → Visual normality check; scipy.stats.probplot.

"Shapiro-Wilk?" → Normality test; H₀: data is normal.

"Category counts?" → s.value_counts(); include NaN with dropna=False.

"Cardinality?" → s.nunique().

"Bimodal histogram?" → Hidden categorical inside; investigate.

"Date range?" → dates.min() to dates.max(); check for gaps.

"Most informative single plot?" → Histogram + boxplot + Q-Q together.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Univariate = one column at a time; first step of EDA
  • Central tendency: mean (sensitive), median (robust)
  • Spread: std (sensitive), IQR / MAD (robust)
  • Shape: skewness (asymmetry), kurtosis (tailedness)
  • |skew| > 1 suggests a log transform
  • Heavy kurtosis suggests outliers; consider robust methods or winsorize
  • Q-Q plot is the most informative normality diagnostic
  • Normality tests over-reject on large samples — use plots instead
  • For categoricals: value_counts, nunique, entropy
  • Pie charts work only for < 5 categories; bar charts otherwise
  • Bimodal distributions often hide a categorical variable
  • Date columns: check range, gaps, and frequency by year/month/day
  • Build a per-column summary table to scan all features quickly
  • Univariate findings drive transform decisions: log, scale, drop, encode
  • Use boxplot, histogram, KDE, and Q-Q together for the full picture

Worked example

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what a single column is telling you, and what it hides
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from scipy import stats
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
normal = pd.Series(rng.normal(170, 8, 2000), name="height_cm")
skewed = pd.Series(rng.lognormal(3.2, 0.8, 2000), name="basket_value")
bimodal = pd.Series(np.concatenate([rng.normal(25, 4, 1000), rng.normal(60, 6, 1000)]), name="age")

print("1. Mean and median agree only when the shape is symmetric.")
for s in (normal, skewed, bimodal):
    print(f"   {s.name:13} mean {s.mean():7.2f}   median {s.median():7.2f}"
          f"   diff {abs(s.mean()-s.median()):6.2f}   skew {s.skew():+.2f}")
print("   basket_value's mean sits well above its median: a few large baskets drag it.")
print("   Quote the median for money, and say so.")

print("\n2. Spread: sd assumes symmetry, IQR does not.")
for s in (normal, skewed):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75])
    print(f"   {s.name:13} sd {s.std():7.2f}   IQR {q3-q1:7.2f}   MAD {stats.median_abs_deviation(s):7.2f}")
print("   For the skewed column the sd is inflated by the tail; the IQR describes where")
print("   the middle half actually sits.")

print("\n3. A histogram is a table. Here is the table.")
counts, edges = np.histogram(normal, bins=8)
for i, c in enumerate(counts):
    bar = "#" * int(c / counts.max() * 40)
    print(f"   {edges[i]:6.1f}-{edges[i+1]:6.1f} {c:>5} {bar}")
print("   Bin count changes the story. Too few hides structure; too many shows noise.")
for b in (3, 8, 40):
    c, _ = np.histogram(bimodal, bins=b)
    peaks = sum(1 for i in range(1, len(c)-1) if c[i] > c[i-1] and c[i] > c[i+1])
    print(f"   bimodal with {b:>2} bins -> {peaks} visible peak(s)")
print("   With 3 bins the two populations in 'age' vanish entirely. That is why you")
print("   always look at more than one binning before concluding anything.")

print("\n4. The five-number summary, and the boxplot it draws.")
for s in (normal, skewed):
    mn, q1, med, q3, mx = s.min(), *s.quantile([.25, .5, .75]), s.max()
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr
    out = ((s < lo) | (s > hi)).sum()
    print(f"   {s.name:13} min {mn:8.2f}  Q1 {q1:8.2f}  med {med:8.2f}  Q3 {q3:8.2f}  max {mx:8.2f}")
    print(f"   {'':13} whiskers [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}] -> {out} points drawn as outliers ({out/len(s)*100:.1f}%)")
print("   A boxplot of a bimodal column looks unremarkable - it only shows quartiles.")
print("   That is the case where you must look at the histogram too.")

print("\n5. Is it normal? Test it rather than assuming.")
for s in (normal, skewed, bimodal):
    stat, p = stats.shapiro(s.sample(500, random_state=0))
    print(f"   {s.name:13} Shapiro-Wilk W={stat:.4f}  p={p:.2e}  "
          f"{'consistent with normal' if p > 0.05 else 'NOT normal'}")
print("   The genuinely normal sample passes; the skewed and bimodal ones are rejected")
print("   overwhelmingly (p around 1e-29 and 1e-21). But note WHY that is so decisive:")
print("   at large n these tests detect departures far too small to matter in practice,")
print("   so a rejection does not mean 'unusable' - it means 'not exactly normal', which")
print("   real data never is. Use the test as a hint and the histogram as the evidence.")
q = np.quantile(normal, [.05,.25,.5,.75,.95])
t = stats.norm.ppf([.05,.25,.5,.75,.95], normal.mean(), normal.std())
print(f"   observed quantiles {np.round(q,1)}")
print(f"   normal-theory      {np.round(t,1)}   max gap {np.abs(q-t).max():.2f}")

print("\n6. Transform a skewed column and watch the shape change.")
logged = np.log1p(skewed)
print(f"   raw   skew {skewed.skew():+.2f}   mean {skewed.mean():.2f}  median {skewed.median():.2f}")
print(f"   log1p skew {logged.skew():+.2f}   mean {logged.mean():.2f}  median {logged.median():.2f}")
print("   Log makes the distribution symmetric - which helps models that assume it - but")
print("   the units are now log-units. Always transform back before reporting a number")
print(f"   to a person: expm1(mean of logs) = {np.expm1(logged.mean()):.2f}, which is the")
print(f"   GEOMETRIC mean, not the arithmetic one ({skewed.mean():.2f}).")

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Bivariate analysis examines pairs of variables — feature-feature and feature-target relationships. It surfaces the strongest predictors, redundant columns, and interaction patterns. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests scatter plots, correlation matrices, group-by visualizations, and chi-square independence.

Numeric vs numeric — correlation + scatter

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Pearson — linear relationships
df.corr()['target'].abs().sort_values(ascending=False)
# Top correlations with the target

# Spearman — monotonic (rank-based)
df.corr(method='spearman')['target'].abs().sort_values(ascending=False)
# Catches non-linear monotonic relationships

# Kendall tau — also rank-based, more robust on small samples
df.corr(method='kendall')

# Scatter plot — the fundamental bivariate visualization
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='income', y='spend', alpha=0.5)

# With regression line
sns.regplot(data=df, x='income', y='spend')

# Color by category (3-way visualization)
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='income', y='spend', hue='product_tier', alpha=0.6)

Correlation matrix — find clusters and redundancy

import numpy as np

corr = df.select_dtypes(include='number').corr()

# Heatmap
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='RdBu_r', center=0,
 vmin=-1, vmax=1, square=True)

# Mask upper triangle for less clutter
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool))
sns.heatmap(corr, mask=mask, annot=True, cmap='RdBu_r', center=0)

# Find highly correlated PAIRS (redundancy candidates)
def find_correlated(df, threshold=0.9):
 corr = df.corr().abs()
 upper = corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
 pairs = []
 for col in upper.columns:
 for idx in upper.index:
 val = upper.loc[idx, col]
 if pd.notna(val) and val > threshold:
 pairs.append((idx, col, val))
 return pd.DataFrame(pairs, columns=['feature_1', 'feature_2', 'correlation'])

find_correlated(df, threshold=0.9)
# Pairs with r > 0.9 — likely redundant; pick one to keep

Numeric vs categorical — group statistics

# Summary per group
df.groupby('product_category')['price'].agg(['count', 'mean', 'median', 'std'])

# Quick visualization
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)

# Violin — more shape info
sns.violinplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price')

# Strip with quartile lines
sns.stripplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price', alpha=0.4, jitter=True)
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price', showfliers=False, ax=plt.gca())

# Bar with means + error bars
sns.barplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price', errorbar='ci')

# Test if group means differ — ANOVA
from scipy.stats import f_oneway
groups = [group['price'].values for name, group in df.groupby('product_category')]
f_stat, p = f_oneway(*groups)
print(f"F = {f_stat:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}")
# p < 0.05 → at least one group differs from the rest

Categorical vs categorical — crosstabs and chi-square

from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

# Contingency table
ct = pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier'])
print(ct)

# Proportions
ct_prop = pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier'], normalize='index')
print(ct_prop)
# Each row sums to 1; shows tier distribution within each city

# Visualize
sns.heatmap(ct, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='viridis')

# Chi-square test of independence
chi2, p, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(ct)
print(f"χ² = {chi2:.2f}, df = {dof}, p = {p:.4f}")
# H₀: city and tier are independent
# p < 0.05 → significantly associated

# Effect size: Cramér's V
n = ct.values.sum()
cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * min(ct.shape) - 1))
print(f"Cramér's V = {cramers_v:.3f}")
# 0 = no association; 1 = perfect; 0.1/0.3/0.5 = small/medium/large

Feature-target analysis — the main goal of bivariate EDA

# For classification: separation per class
# Numeric feature vs binary target
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='churned', y='tenure')
sns.histplot(data=df, x='tenure', hue='churned', element='step', stat='density')

# For categorical feature vs target — bar of mean(target) per category
df.groupby('product_tier')['churned'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False).plot(kind='bar')
plt.ylabel('Churn rate')
plt.title('Churn rate by product tier')

# Mutual information (captures any kind of relationship)
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif, mutual_info_regression

X = df.drop('target', axis=1).select_dtypes(include='number')
y = df['target']

mi = mutual_info_classif(X, y, random_state=42)
mi_series = pd.Series(mi, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(mi_series.head(10))
# Higher = stronger relationship; works for linear AND non-linear

Pairwise visualization — pairplot and clustermap

import seaborn as sns

# Pairplot — all pairwise scatters + diagonals
sns.pairplot(df[['age', 'income', 'spend', 'target']], hue='target', diag_kind='kde')

# Limit to important columns — pairplot is O(n_features²)

# Cluster map — group similar columns together
sns.clustermap(corr, annot=True, cmap='RdBu_r', center=0)
# Reorders rows/cols by similarity; reveals natural groups of correlated features

# Color sidebar for column types
col_colors = pd.Series(X.dtypes).map({
 'int64': 'red', 'float64': 'blue', 'object': 'green'
})
sns.clustermap(corr, row_colors=col_colors)

Interaction plots

# Does the effect of one feature depend on another?

# Means by combination of factors
sns.pointplot(data=df, x='product_tier', y='churned', hue='region')
# Parallel lines → no interaction
# Crossing or diverging lines → interaction

# Heatmap of mean target by two categoricals
pivot = df.pivot_table(index='product_tier', columns='region', values='churned', aggfunc='mean')
sns.heatmap(pivot, annot=True, fmt='.3f', cmap='coolwarm', center=0.5)

# Quick test for interaction via groupby
df.groupby(['product_tier', 'region'])['churned'].mean().unstack()

Worked example — full bivariate EDA

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Customer churn EDA
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency, f_oneway

# Step 1: correlation matrix for numeric
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(df.select_dtypes(include='number').corr(),
 annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='RdBu_r', center=0)
plt.title('Numeric feature correlations')
plt.show()

# Step 2: numeric features vs target
numeric_features = ['age', 'tenure', 'monthly_spend', 'support_tickets']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
for ax, feat in zip(axes.flat, numeric_features):
 sns.boxplot(data=df, x='churned', y=feat, ax=ax)
 ax.set_title(f'{feat} by churn')

 # ANOVA p-value
 groups = [df[df['churned'] == c][feat].dropna() for c in [0, 1]]
 f, p = f_oneway(*groups)
 ax.set_xlabel(f'churned (ANOVA p = {p:.3f})')
plt.tight_layout()

# Step 3: categorical features vs target
cat_features = ['city', 'product_tier', 'plan_type']
for feat in cat_features:
 # Mean churn rate per category
 rates = df.groupby(feat)['churned'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
 rates.plot(kind='bar', figsize=(10, 4))
 plt.title(f'Churn rate by {feat}')
 plt.ylabel('Churn rate')
 plt.show()

 # Chi-square test
 ct = pd.crosstab(df[feat], df['churned'])
 chi2, p, dof, _ = chi2_contingency(ct)
 print(f"{feat}: χ² = {chi2:.1f}, p = {p:.4f}")

# Step 4: top mutual-info features
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder

X_for_mi = df.drop('churned', axis=1).copy()
# Encode categoricals so MI can use them
for col in X_for_mi.select_dtypes(include='object'):
 X_for_mi[col] = OrdinalEncoder().fit_transform(X_for_mi[[col]])
X_for_mi = X_for_mi.fillna(-1)

mi = mutual_info_classif(X_for_mi, df['churned'], random_state=42)
mi_series = pd.Series(mi, index=X_for_mi.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(mi_series.head(10))
# Top features by MI — candidate predictors regardless of relationship shape

Common bivariate mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Trusting Pearson when the relationship is non-linear — use Spearman or MI
  2. Reading correlation as causation
  3. Forgetting to handle high cardinality categoricals — chi-square test fails with sparse cells
  4. Pairplot on 50+ columns — explodes; select top features first
  5. Comparing means without checking variances — heteroscedastic comparison is misleading
  6. Confidence in p < 0.05 with huge data — practically tiny associations are "significant"
  7. Missing the leakage tell: a feature with |r| > 0.95 with target — probably leakage
  8. Categorical with too many values for chi-square — combine rare categories or use mutual info
  9. Hidden interactions — main effects of A and B may be tiny but the AB interaction huge
  10. Bivariate analysis without missing-value handling — NaN distorts everything
★ ON THE EXAM

"Numeric vs numeric?" → Scatter plot + Pearson/Spearman correlation.

"Pearson vs Spearman?" → Pearson is linear; Spearman is rank-based (monotonic).

"Numeric vs categorical?" → Boxplot per group + ANOVA.

"Categorical vs categorical?" → Crosstab + chi-square + Cramér's V.

"Feature-target with non-linear?" → Mutual information (sklearn).

"Find redundant features?" → Correlation matrix; pairs with |r| > 0.9.

"Pairplot purpose?" → All pairwise scatter plots in one grid.

"Interaction visualization?" → Pointplot with hue, or pivot heatmap.

"Cramér's V?" → Effect size for chi-square; 0=no association, 1=perfect.

"Suspicious very-high correlation with target?" → Possible data leakage.

"Best test for any relationship type?" → Mutual information.

"Big n + tiny correlation significant?" → Statistically yes, practically no.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Bivariate analysis examines pairs of variables to find relationships
  • Numeric-numeric: Pearson (linear), Spearman (monotonic), scatter plot
  • Numeric-categorical: boxplot per group + ANOVA
  • Categorical-categorical: crosstab + chi-square + Cramér's V
  • Mutual information captures any relationship type, including non-linear
  • Correlation matrix surfaces redundant features (|r| > 0.9) and target-correlated features
  • Pearson r is sensitive to outliers; Spearman uses ranks and is robust
  • Feature-target bivariate is the most important kind of EDA — drives feature selection
  • Visualize bivariate relationships before trusting summary numbers (Anscombe's quartet)
  • For class-target visual diagnostics: boxplot, histplot with hue, mean target per category
  • Suspiciously high correlation with the target → suspect data leakage
  • Always check missing values BEFORE bivariate analysis — NaN distorts everything
  • For big data, prefer effect size over p-values (statistical vs practical significance)
  • Interaction plots reveal effects that single-feature analysis misses
  • Clustermap groups correlated features visually — useful for natural groupings

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The target variable is the most important column in any supervised learning project. Its distribution determines the metric you'll use, the resampling strategy you'll need, and whether the problem is even feasible. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests recognizing class imbalance, target skew, and target-feature relationships.

Classification — class balance

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Counts
df['target'].value_counts()

# Proportions
df['target'].value_counts(normalize=True)
# 0 0.85
# 1 0.15

# Visualize
df['target'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.title('Target class distribution')

# Imbalance ratio
counts = df['target'].value_counts()
ratio = counts.max() / counts.min()
print(f"Imbalance ratio: {ratio:.1f}:1")

Classifying the imbalance

Ratio (majority:minority)SeverityApproach
~50:50 to 65:35BalancedUse accuracy; no special handling
65:35 to 90:10Mildly imbalancedF1, ROC AUC; class_weight='balanced'
90:10 to 99:1Severely imbalancedPR AUC; SMOTE; cost-sensitive learning
More extremeRare eventAnomaly detection; one-class methods

The trivial baseline

# A model that always predicts the majority class gives accuracy = majority proportion
majority_class = df['target'].mode()[0]
trivial_accuracy = (df['target'] == majority_class).mean()
print(f"Trivial accuracy: {trivial_accuracy:.3f}")

# Any model you train MUST beat this — otherwise it's adding nothing

# Examples:
# 50/50 → trivial accuracy 0.50
# 90/10 → trivial accuracy 0.90 (impressive sounding but useless!)
# 99/1 → trivial accuracy 0.99 (model adds zero value if it matches this)

# For imbalanced data, use class_weight='balanced' or resample
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced', max_iter=1000)

Multi-class targets

df['target_3class'].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index().plot(kind='bar')
plt.ylabel('Proportion')

Information value (IV) — for binary classification

import numpy as np

# IV measures predictive power of categorical (or binned numeric) features
# Used in credit scoring, churn, and other binary classification problems

def information_value(df, feature, target):
 """Compute IV between feature and binary target."""
 # Bins for numeric features
 if df[feature].dtype.kind in 'biufc':
 df = df.copy()
 df[feature] = pd.qcut(df[feature], q=10, duplicates='drop')

 crosstab = pd.crosstab(df[feature], df[target])
 crosstab.columns = ['non_event', 'event']

 crosstab['p_event'] = crosstab['event'] / crosstab['event'].sum()
 crosstab['p_non_event'] = crosstab['non_event'] / crosstab['non_event'].sum()
 crosstab['woe'] = np.log(crosstab['p_event'] / crosstab['p_non_event'])
 crosstab['iv_part'] = (crosstab['p_event'] - crosstab['p_non_event']) * crosstab['woe']

 return crosstab['iv_part'].sum()

# IV thresholds (credit scoring convention):
# < 0.02: Unhelpful
# 0.02-0.1: Weak predictor
# 0.1-0.3: Medium
# 0.3-0.5: Strong
# > 0.5: Suspiciously strong (possible leakage)

# Compute for all features
features = df.columns.drop('target')
iv_results = {feat: information_value(df, feat, 'target') for feat in features}
pd.Series(iv_results).sort_values(ascending=False).head(15)

Common target-analysis mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data — use F1, ROC AUC, PR AUC instead
  2. Not computing the trivial baseline — you don't know if you're adding value
  3. Imputing the target — drop those rows instead
  4. Ignoring target outliers in regression — they dominate MSE
  5. Trying to model heavily skewed target without transforming — linear assumptions break
  6. Forgetting to inverse-transform predictions after log transform
  7. Treating target as numeric when it's ordinal categorical — use ordinal regression
  8. Cross-validating without stratify on imbalanced classification
  9. Computing IV without binning numeric features — IV needs discrete bins
  10. Mistaking an IV > 0.5 for great predictor — often actually data leakage
★ ON THE EXAM

"Class balance check?" → df['target'].value_counts(normalize=True).

"Imbalance ratio?" → max count ÷ min count.

"Trivial baseline?" → Majority-class proportion (= accuracy of always predicting majority).

"Mildly imbalanced metric?" → F1, ROC AUC.

"Severely imbalanced metric?" → PR AUC.

"Sklearn class weighting?" → class_weight='balanced'.

"Skewed regression target?" → Log transform (np.log1p); invert with np.expm1.

"Skewness threshold?" → |skew| > 1 suggests transform.

"Information Value (IV)?" → Credit-scoring measure of predictive power; 0.1-0.3 medium.

"Always plot target?" → Yes, before modeling.

"Drop missing target?" → Always; never impute.

"CV on imbalanced classification?" → StratifiedKFold.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • The target distribution determines the metric, sampling strategy, and feasibility
  • For classification, compute class proportions and imbalance ratio FIRST
  • Always compute the trivial baseline (majority class accuracy)
  • Balanced (50/50): use accuracy; mildly imbalanced: F1 or ROC AUC; severely: PR AUC
  • For severe imbalance, consider SMOTE, class_weight='balanced', or anomaly detection framing
  • For regression, plot histogram + Q-Q + boxplot of the target first
  • |skew| > 1 → consider log or Box-Cox transform
  • After log-transforming y, remember to inverse-transform predictions
  • Outliers in the target dominate MSE — use robust loss (MAE, Huber) if keeping them
  • For classification: plot each feature's distribution per class to see which separate the classes
  • For regression: scatter each feature vs target to see relationship strength and shape
  • For categorical features: bar chart of mean target rate per category
  • Information Value (IV) is a credit-scoring metric for predictor strength
  • IV > 0.5 often means data leakage — investigate before celebrating
  • Always drop rows where the target is missing — never impute the target

Univariate looks at one variable, bivariate at pairs — multivariate considers many at once. Real datasets have 10-100+ features and the interesting patterns often involve combinations. Why go beyond pairs

★ MULTIVARIATE PATTERNS

Patterns invisible in univariate or bivariate analysis:

  • Two features each weakly predict the target, but their INTERACTION is strong
  • Three features are individually correlated, but only two add information (collinearity)

  • An outlier in 2D may be perfectly normal in each individual dimension

Multicollinearity check

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Find clusters of correlated features
corr = df.select_dtypes(include='number').corr().abs()

# Find pairs with high correlation
def find_correlated_pairs(corr, threshold=0.9):
 upper = corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
 pairs = []
 for c in upper.columns:
 for r in upper.index:
 val = upper.loc[r, c]
 if pd.notna(val) and val > threshold:
 pairs.append((r, c, val))
 return pd.DataFrame(pairs, columns=['f1', 'f2', 'corr'])

high_corr = find_correlated_pairs(corr, 0.9)
print(high_corr)

# Variance Inflation Factor — formal multicollinearity diagnostic
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

X_for_vif = df.select_dtypes(include='number').dropna()
vif = pd.DataFrame({
 'feature': X_for_vif.columns,
 'VIF': [variance_inflation_factor(X_for_vif.values, i) for i in range(X_for_vif.shape[1])]
})
print(vif.sort_values('VIF', ascending=False))

# VIF interpretation:
# 1 — no collinearity
# 1-5 — moderate
# 5-10 — high; consider removing
# > 10 — severe; one of the features should go

Common multivariate mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Pairplot on 50 features — explodes to 2500 panels
  2. PCA without scaling — largest-variance feature dominates
  3. Trusting t-SNE distances — they don't preserve global structure
  4. Skipping multicollinearity check — leads to unstable linear models
  5. Confusing PCA components with original features — PCs are linear combinations
  6. Ignoring interactions when models are linear — RF/GB handle them; linear doesn't
  7. Treating cluster IDs as ordered — they're arbitrary labels
  8. Comparing cluster IDs across runs — same data → different labels
  9. Using parallel coordinates without scaling — one column dominates visually
  10. Reading too much into t-SNE / UMAP cluster shapes — artifacts of the algorithm
★ ON THE EXAM

"All pairwise in one image?" → sns.pairplot.

"Many features, one observation per line?" → Parallel coordinates.

"Dimensionality reduction for visualization?" → PCA (linear), t-SNE / UMAP (non-linear).

"PCA before what?" → Always scale features first.

"PCA components?" → Linear combinations of original features ordered by variance.

"explained_variance_ratio_?" → Fraction of total variance per PC.

"t-SNE caveat?" → Distances don't preserve global structure; tune perplexity.

"Clustering for exploration?" → KMeans for spherical, DBSCAN for arbitrary shapes.

"Variance Inflation Factor?" → Multicollinearity diagnostic; > 5 is concerning.

"Interaction visualization?" → Faceted lmplot or pointplot with hue.

"Quick feature importance?" → Fit RandomForest, inspect feature_importances_.

"5+ dimensions in one plot?" → Use color, size, shape, AND facets sparingly.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Multivariate analysis examines many features simultaneously — often reveals patterns invisible in pairs
  • Add dimensions to a scatter plot via hue, size, and style (up to 5 vars)
  • Pairplot shows all pairwise scatters + diagonals; limit to top features (O(n²))
  • Parallel coordinates: each row becomes a line connecting feature values; scale first
  • PCA reduces dimensions linearly while preserving variance; always scale before PCA
  • t-SNE / UMAP reveal non-linear cluster structure but distort distances
  • Cluster IDs from k-means or DBSCAN segment the data for further analysis
  • VIF > 5 indicates multicollinearity — drop one of the correlated features
  • For high-cardinality feature sets, fit a quick RandomForest for importance rankings
  • Interaction detection: faceted lmplot or pointplot with hue
  • Tree-based models capture interactions automatically; linear models need explicit interactions
  • Use PCA loadings (components_) to interpret what each PC represents
  • Cluster summaries (mean of each feature per cluster) make segments interpretable
  • Pairplot and PCA together are a strong starter combo for any new dataset
  • Always combine multiple techniques: visual + statistical + model-based

Outlier detection three ways: the IQR rule — keep rows between Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR on the amount column, filter the rest; the z-score — (x − mean) / std, flagging |z| > 3; and sklearn’s IsolationForest — a model-based detector that flags multivariate outliers a single column’s rule would miss.

EDA isn't done until you've communicated what you found. A great EDA produces a clear narrative for stakeholders - what's in the data, what's notable, what to investigate next, what to act on.

What goes in an EDA report

  • Context: what is this dataset, where did it come from, what's the goal?
  • Shape and structure: how many rows/columns? what does each column mean?
  • Quality: missing data, outliers, duplicates, type issues - and how you handled them.
  • Key findings: 3-5 main takeaways with charts to support each.
  • Suspicious patterns: things that need follow-up.
  • Recommendations: what to do next - more data? specific models? data fixes?
  • Audience matters - executive summary differs from technical handoff.

Communicating to stakeholders

# Translate technical findings to business language

# Bad: "P-value of t-test for income difference between churners and 
# non-churners is 0.003, with Cohen's d of 0.31"

# Good: "Customers who churned earned $8K less on average ($52K vs $60K).
# This pattern is statistically significant and unlikely to be due to chance."

# Use comparisons to known things
# Bad: "AUC of 0.78 on the validation set"
# Good: "Our model correctly ranks a churner higher than a non-churner
# 78% of the time. By comparison, random would be 50% and perfect 100%."

# Always include actionability
# Findings -> implications -> recommended actions
# "Tenure < 6 months has 42% churn (3x baseline)"
# -> "New customers are at much higher risk"
# -> "Recommend: increase onboarding outreach in first 6 months"
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Don't bury the lede. Stakeholders skim - put the headline finding first, then evidence. Don't include every chart you made - pick 5 that tell the story. The rest belong in an appendix or supplementary notebook.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — turning findings into something a reader can act on
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)

rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
n = 1200
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "channel": rng.choice(["email", "search", "social", "direct"], n, p=[.35, .3, .25, .1]),
    "spend":   rng.gamma(2, 40, n).round(2),
    "signup":  rng.random(n)})
df["converted"] = (df["signup"] < np.where(df["channel"] == "email", .28, .15)).astype(int)
df.loc[rng.choice(n, 90, replace=False), "spend"] = np.nan

print("1. Start from the question, not the data.")
print("   'Which channel should get next quarter's budget?' is answerable.")
print("   'What is in this dataset?' is not, and produces 40 charts nobody reads.")

print("\n2. The finding, stated as a number with its uncertainty.")
g = df.groupby("channel").agg(users=("converted", "size"),
                              conversions=("converted", "sum"),
                              rate=("converted", "mean"))
g["rate_pct"] = (g["rate"] * 100).round(1)
# Wald interval - enough for a report, and it shows how wide small samples are
se = np.sqrt(g["rate"] * (1 - g["rate"]) / g["users"])
g["ci_low"] = ((g["rate"] - 1.96 * se) * 100).round(1)
g["ci_high"] = ((g["rate"] + 1.96 * se) * 100).round(1)
print(g[["users", "conversions", "rate_pct", "ci_low", "ci_high"]].to_string())
print("   Email converts highest. The intervals are what stop this being overclaimed:")
lo_e, hi_e = g.loc["email", ["ci_low", "ci_high"]]
lo_d, hi_d = g.loc["direct", ["ci_low", "ci_high"]]
print(f"   email  {g.loc['email','rate_pct']}% [{lo_e}, {hi_e}]")
print(f"   direct {g.loc['direct','rate_pct']}% [{lo_d}, {hi_d}]  <- {int(g.loc['direct','users'])} users, so a wide interval")
print(f"   overlapping intervals? {'yes' if lo_e <= hi_d and lo_d <= hi_e else 'no'}")

print("\n3. Say what you did to the data. Every number depends on it.")
notes = [f"rows: {len(df):,}",
         f"spend missing: {df['spend'].isna().sum()} ({df['spend'].isna().mean()*100:.1f}%) - left as NaN, not imputed",
         f"conversion = signup < channel threshold (simulated for this example)",
         f"intervals: 95% Wald normal approximation",
         "no rows excluded"]
for x in notes: print(f"   - {x}")

print("\n4. One table beats five charts. Rank it, and put the decision column last.")
summary = (g.assign(share_of_users=(g["users"] / g["users"].sum() * 100).round(1))
             .sort_values("rate_pct", ascending=False)
             [["users", "share_of_users", "rate_pct", "ci_low", "ci_high"]])
print(summary.to_string())

print("\n5. Write the three sentences that a reader will actually remember.")
best = summary.index[0]; worst = summary.index[-1]
print(f"   1. {best} converts at {summary.loc[best,'rate_pct']}%, the highest of the four channels,")
print(f"      on {int(summary.loc[best,'users']):,} users - the largest group, so the estimate is the firmest.")
print(f"   2. {worst} is lowest at {summary.loc[worst,'rate_pct']}%, but on only {int(summary.loc[worst,'users'])} users;")
print(f"      its interval [{summary.loc[worst,'ci_low']}, {summary.loc[worst,'ci_high']}] overlaps two other channels, so it is not")
print("      safely distinguishable from them yet.")
print("   3. Recommend shifting budget toward the leader and collecting more data on the")
print("      smallest channel before cutting it.")

print("\n6. What NOT to put in the report.")
for x in ["every chart you made while exploring - keep the ones that changed your mind",
          "a correlation matrix with no comment on which cells matter",
          "raw code output pasted in - a reader wants the number, not the dtype listing",
          "a conclusion the intervals do not support",
          "'further analysis is needed' with no statement of what it would settle"]:
    print(f"   - {x}")

print("\n7. The honesty check, before you send it.")
for q in ["Would this conclusion survive if I removed the largest group?",
          "Does any claim rest on a group with fewer than ~30 observations?",
          "Have I said which rows I dropped, and why?",
          "Am I reporting a correlation as though it were a cause?"]:
    print(f"   ? {q}")
small = summary[summary["users"] < 200]
print(f"   groups under 200 users here: {list(small.index) or 'none'}")

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

"Garbage in, garbage out" — most failed ML projects fail at data quality, not algorithm choice. Data cleaning is the bulk of real-world data work. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests removing duplicates, fixing dtypes, parsing dates, normalizing strings, and handling categorical inconsistencies.

The cleaning checklist

★ DATA CLEANING ORDER
  1. Inspect: understand the raw data first
  2. Fix dtypes: parse dates, convert numerics, normalize strings
  3. Standardize values: trim whitespace, fix case, normalize categories
  4. Drop duplicates after standardization (so spelling diffs don't hide them)
  5. Handle missing: drop, impute, or flag (per ML ch2)
  6. Outlier review: keep or cap or transform
  7. Sanity checks: ranges, dates, references valid
  8. Document: record every change made

Fixing dtypes

import pandas as pd

# Pandas often guesses wrong on load — check df.dtypes after read_csv

# String → numeric
df['price'] = pd.to_numeric(df['price'], errors='coerce')
# errors='coerce' turns unparseable values to NaN
# errors='raise' (default) errors out
# errors='ignore' leaves unchanged

# Cast columns explicitly
df = df.astype({
 'order_id': 'int64',
 'category': 'category', # huge memory savings on repeated strings
 'price': 'float64'
})

# Booleans from strings
df['active'] = df['active'].map({'yes': True, 'no': False, 'y': True, 'n': False})

# Strings → datetime
df['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['order_date'], errors='coerce')
df['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['order_date'], format='%Y-%m-%d')

# Memory check
df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1024**2 # MB
# Converting object → category often cuts memory by 10x+

import pandas as pd

# Strip whitespace
df['city'] = df['city'].str.strip() # leading/trailing
df['city'] = df['city'].str.replace(r'\s+', ' ', regex=True) # collapse internal

# Case normalization
df['city'] = df['city'].str.lower() # for matching
df['city'] = df['city'].str.title() # "New York" style

df['name'] = df['name'].str.replace(r'[^A-Za-z\s]', '', regex=True)

Outliers — keep, cap, or transform

import numpy as np

# Option 1: KEEP — they may be legitimate (genuine high spenders)
# No action

# Option 2: CAP / WINSORIZE — replace with percentile values
def winsorize(s, lower=0.01, upper=0.99):
 low = s.quantile(lower)
 high = s.quantile(upper)
 return s.clip(low, high)

df['income'] = winsorize(df['income'])
# Or scipy: stats.mstats.winsorize(df['income'], limits=[0.01, 0.01])

# Option 3: TRANSFORM — log/sqrt makes outliers less extreme
df['log_income'] = np.log1p(df['income'])

# Option 4: REMOVE — only when you're sure they're errors
mask = (df['income'] > 10_000_000) | (df['income'] < 0)
df = df[~mask]

The cleaning function pattern

# Wrap cleaning logic in a pure, testable function
def clean_customer_data(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
 df = df.copy()

 # 1. Trim and lowercase strings
 for col in df.select_dtypes(include='object'):
 df[col] = df[col].str.strip()

 # 2. Parse dates
 for col in ['signup_date', 'last_order_date']:
 df[col] = pd.to_datetime(df[col], errors='coerce')

 # 3. Convert numerics
 df['income'] = pd.to_numeric(df['income'], errors='coerce')

 # 4. Standardize cities
 df['city'] = df['city'].str.title()
 df['city'] = df['city'].replace({'Nyc': 'New York', 'La': 'Los Angeles'})

 # 5. Sanity checks
 df.loc[df['age'] < 0, 'age'] = pd.NA
 df.loc[df['age'] > 120, 'age'] = pd.NA

 # 6. Drop duplicates
 df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['customer_id'])

 return df

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Raw — many problems
df = pd.DataFrame({
 'id': ['1', '2', '3', '4', '4', '5'],
 'name': ['Alice', ' Bob', 'CHARLIE', 'Dana ', 'Dana ', 'Eve'],
 'email': ['alice@e.com', 'bob@e.com', 'CHARLIE@E.COM', 'dana@e.com', 'dana@e.com', 'eve@e.com'],
 'age': ['25', '32', '-1', '45', '45', '999'],
 'city': ['NYC', 'n.y.', 'L.A.', 'CHICAGO', 'CHICAGO', 'NY'],
 'date': ['2024-01-15', '01/20/2024', '2024-02-30', '2024-03-10', '2024-03-10', 'invalid'],

})

def clean(df):
 df = df.copy()

 # Strip strings
 for col in df.select_dtypes(include='object'):
 df[col] = df[col].str.strip()

 # ID to int
 df['id'] = pd.to_numeric(df['id'], errors='coerce').astype('Int64')

 # Email standardize
 df['email'] = df['email'].str.lower()

 # Name title-case
 df['name'] = df['name'].str.title()

 # Age parse + sanity
 df['age'] = pd.to_numeric(df['age'], errors='coerce')
 df.loc[(df['age'] < 0) | (df['age'] > 120), 'age'] = pd.NA

 # City normalize
 df['city'] = df['city'].str.upper().str.replace('.', '', regex=False)
 df['city'] = df['city'].replace({'NYC': 'NEW YORK', 'NY': 'NEW YORK', 'LA': 'LOS ANGELES'})

 # Date parse (mixed formats)
 df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'], errors='coerce', format='mixed')

 # Income parse
 df['income'] = (df['income'].astype(str)
 .str.replace(r'[$,]', '', regex=True)
 .str.replace('?', '', regex=False))
 df['income'] = pd.to_numeric(df['income'], errors='coerce')

 # Drop duplicates by id
 df = df.drop_duplicates(subset='id')

 return df

clean_df = clean(df)

Common data cleaning mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Cleaning on the full dataset before train/test split — but: cleaning that doesn't use statistics is fine; imputation/scaling shouldn't
  2. Dropping duplicates BEFORE standardizing — misses "Alice" vs "ALICE" duplicates
  3. Forgetting errors='coerce' in to_numeric / to_datetime — script crashes on first bad row
  4. Treating "0" as missing — sometimes zero is meaningful
  5. Capping outliers without thinking — sometimes legitimate big values matter
  6. Mixing dtypes in the same column — int + float + NaN → object; coerce to one type
  7. Not documenting changes — future you won't remember why rows disappeared
  8. Using inplace=True — harder to chain, easier to silently modify caller
  9. Forgetting timezone — naive vs aware datetime can crash on comparison
  10. Treating cleaning as one-time — wrap in a function, version-control it
★ ON THE EXAM

"Convert string to numeric, ignore errors?" → pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce').

"Parse dates?" → pd.to_datetime(s, errors='coerce').

"Strip whitespace?" → s.str.strip().

"Lowercase?" → s.str.lower().

"Replace values?" → s.replace({'old': 'new'}).

"Drop duplicates?" → df.drop_duplicates(subset=cols).

"Cast types?" → df.astype({'col': 'category'}).

"Save memory on repeated strings?" → Convert to category dtype.

"Cap outliers (winsorize)?" → s.clip(low, high).

"Extract phone area code?" → s.str.extract(r'(\d{3})').

"Reusable cleaning?" → Wrap in a function; call on train and test separately.

"Fuzzy match for categories?" → fuzzywuzzy.process.extractOne.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Data cleaning is the largest time sink in any real ML project — make it reproducible
  • Wrap cleaning logic in a pure function so it's testable and rerunnable
  • Standard order: inspect → fix dtypes → standardize strings → drop duplicates → handle missing → outliers → sanity → document
  • Use pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce') to convert with NaN for bad values
  • Use pd.to_datetime(..., errors='coerce') for date parsing
  • Strip whitespace and standardize case BEFORE deduplication
  • Replace sentinel values (-999, "NA") with proper NaN
  • Cast repeated string columns to category dtype for huge memory savings
  • Sanity-check ranges: negative ages, future dates, foreign key integrity
  • Outliers: keep, cap (winsorize with clip), transform (log), or remove — never blindly
  • Standardize units (currency, weight, timezone) before modeling
  • Fuzzy matching via fuzzywuzzy.process for many spelling variations
  • Document the number of rows changed/dropped and the reasoning
  • For ML pipelines, do stat-based cleaning (imputation) inside a Pipeline; do dtype/string cleaning outside
  • Avoid inplace=True — return new DataFrames; easier to chain and debug

Missing data is the most common problem in real datasets. pandas provides a rich set of tools for detecting and handling missing values — but the right choice depends on the column type, the missingness mechanism, and downstream use. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests isna, fillna, dropna, and the difference between pandas NaN and NA.

NaN vs None vs NaT vs pd.NA

ValueTypeUsed for
np.nanfloatMissing numeric (default in pandas)
NoneNoneTypeObject columns; treated as NaN
pd.NaTdatetimeMissing datetime / timedelta
pd.NApandas scalarUniversal missing (newer; for Int64, boolean, etc.)

import pandas as pd

s.isna()

# 1 True
# 2 True
# 3 True
# 4 False

# Use .isna() / .isnull() or pd.isna() to check
np.nan == np.nan # False

Detecting missing values

df.isna().sum() # count per column

# Pattern visualization

Hidden missing values (sentinels)

# Convert them to proper NaN before processing

 -999: np.nan, -1: np.nan,
 'N/A': np.nan, 'NA': np.nan, 'na': np.nan,
 '': np.nan, '?': np.nan, 'unknown': np.nan, 'NULL': np.nan
})

# Often easier to set at read_csv time

# Check minimums and maximums per column to find sentinels
df.describe().T[['min', 'max']]
# A minimum of -999 in age stands out

Dropping missing values

# Drop rows with ANY missing
df.dropna()

# Drop rows missing in SPECIFIC columns
df.dropna(subset=['target']) # critical for ML

# Drop columns missing too much
threshold = 0.5
df = df.loc[:, df.isna().mean() < threshold]

# Keep rows with at least N non-missing values
df.dropna(thresh=df.shape[1] - 3)

# Drop based on combinations (all of these must be missing)
df.dropna(subset=['col_a', 'col_b'], how='all')

# Reset index after drop if you'll index numerically later
df = df.dropna().reset_index(drop=True)

Filling missing values

# Fill with a constant
df['x'].fillna(0)
df['x'].fillna('missing')

# Fill with column statistics
df['age'].fillna(df['age'].median())
df['city'].fillna(df['city'].mode()[0])

# Fill multiple columns differently in one call
df = df.fillna({
 'age': df['age'].median(),
 'income': df['income'].median(),
 'city': 'unknown',
 'is_active': False
})

df['price'].fillna(method='bfill') # use next known

# Linear interpolation

df['price'].interpolate(method='time') # if index is datetime

# Group-wise filling (e.g., per-customer median)

Documenting missing-value handling

★ KEEP A LOG

For each column with missing values, document:

  • Original missing rate
  • Suspected mechanism (MCAR / MAR / MNAR)
  • Strategy chosen (drop / impute / flag+impute)
  • Reasoning
  • Effect on dataset size

Without this, six months later you won't remember why "income" became 100% non-null.

Common missing-value mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Imputing before train/test split — leaks test statistics
  2. Filling with mean on skewed data — use median for prices, incomes, response times
  3. Forgetting to convert sentinels (-999) to NaN first
  4. Dropping rows blindly — losing 40% of data when imputation would work
  5. Using == to check for NaN — always False; use isna()
  6. Imputing the target column — drop those rows instead
  7. Not flagging informative missingness — loses signal in MNAR cases
  8. Using fillna inplace=True when chaining — easy to make mistakes
  9. Forgetting that mode() returns a Series — use .mode()[0] or .iloc[0]
  10. Group-imputing with very small groups — fall back to global median for sparse groups
★ ON THE EXAM

"Detect missing?" → df.isna() or df.isnull() (same).

"Count per column?" → df.isna().sum().

"Rate per column?" → df.isna().mean().

"Drop rows with any missing?" → df.dropna().

"Drop rows where target is missing?" → df.dropna(subset=['target']).

"Fill with median?" → df['col'].fillna(df['col'].median()).

"Different fills per column?" → df.fillna({'a': 0, 'b': 'unknown'}).

"Forward fill?" → df.ffill() (time series only).

"Interpolate?" → df.interpolate(method='linear').

"sklearn imputer?" → SimpleImputer(strategy='median').

"Always check?" → np.nan == np.nan is False; use isna().

"Sentinel -999?" → Replace with np.nan first: df.replace(-999, np.nan).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • pandas treats np.nan, None, pd.NaT, and pd.NA all as "missing"
  • Use isna() / isnull() for detection — never == np.nan
  • Sentinel values (-999, "N/A", "?", empty strings) must be converted to NaN before processing
  • Set na_values in read_csv to catch sentinels at load time
  • Drop rows when target is missing; drop columns > 50% missing with no expected signal
  • For numeric, use median (robust to skew) over mean
  • For categorical, use mode or a "missing" category
  • Forward fill / interpolation for time-series; not for cross-sectional data
  • Group-wise imputation preserves group-level structure (city, customer, etc.)
  • Flag missingness with an indicator column when missingness may be informative
  • Always fit imputers on training data only; transform both train and test
  • Use SimpleImputer in a Pipeline to prevent CV leakage automatically
  • missingno or seaborn heatmap reveal patterns in missingness
  • Document missing-value decisions per column for reproducibility
  • Modern pandas: avoid inplace=True; assign back to the column instead

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — five imputation strategies scored against a truth we planted
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer, KNNImputer
from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer  # noqa: F401
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer
pd.set_option("display.width", 115)

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
n = 600
truth = pd.DataFrame({
    "age":    rng.normal(45, 12, n).round(1),
    "income": None, "score": None})
truth["income"] = (truth["age"] * 900 + rng.normal(0, 6000, n) + 20000).round(0)
truth["score"] = (truth["income"] / 1000 + rng.normal(0, 5, n)).round(2)

print("1. Three ways data goes missing, and only one is safe to ignore.")
print("   MCAR - missing completely at random: a sensor dropped packets.")
print("   MAR  - missingness depends on OTHER columns: older people skip 'income'.")
print("   MNAR - missingness depends on the missing value itself: high earners skip it.")
print("   Only MCAR can be dropped without bias. The other two need thought.")

df = truth.copy()
# MAR: income is missing more often for older rows
p = (df["age"] - df["age"].min()) / (df["age"].max() - df["age"].min()) * 0.5
missing_mask = rng.random(n) < p
df.loc[missing_mask, "income"] = np.nan
print(f"\n   planted MAR missingness: {missing_mask.sum()} of {n} incomes ({missing_mask.mean()*100:.0f}%)")
print(f"   mean age where income is PRESENT {df.loc[~missing_mask,'age'].mean():.1f}")
print(f"   mean age where income is MISSING {df.loc[ missing_mask,'age'].mean():.1f}")
print("   The two differ, which is the fingerprint of MAR: the missingness is not random")
print("   with respect to age, so dropping those rows biases every age-related result.")

print("\n2. What each strategy does to the distribution. Truth is known here, so we can score it.")
true_vals = truth.loc[missing_mask, "income"].values
rows = []
def score(name, filled):
    got = filled[missing_mask]
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((got - true_vals) ** 2)))
    rows.append((name, filled.mean(), filled.std(), rmse,
                 float(np.corrcoef(df["age"], filled)[0, 1])))

score("truth (unknowable)", truth["income"].values.astype(float))
drop_mean = df["income"].dropna().mean()
rows.append(("drop the rows", drop_mean, df["income"].dropna().std(), float("nan"),
             float(np.corrcoef(df.loc[~missing_mask, "age"], df.loc[~missing_mask, "income"])[0, 1])))
for label, strat in [("mean", "mean"), ("median", "median")]:
    filled = SimpleImputer(strategy=strat).fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()
    score(label, filled)
knn = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5).fit_transform(df[["age", "income", "score"]])
score("KNN (k=5)", knn[:, 1])
it = IterativeImputer(random_state=0, max_iter=20).fit_transform(df[["age", "income", "score"]])
score("iterative (model-based)", it[:, 1])

print(f"   {'strategy':24} {'mean':>10} {'std':>10} {'RMSE vs truth':>14} {'corr with age':>14}")
for name, m, s, r, c in rows:
    rs = "     (n/a)" if np.isnan(r) else f"{r:14,.0f}"
    print(f"   {name:24} {m:10,.0f} {s:10,.0f} {rs} {c:14.3f}")

print("\n3. Read that table, because it contains the whole lesson.")
print("   - Dropping the rows shifts the mean downward, because the rows that survive")
print("     are the younger ones - the age composition changed, not the relationship.")
print("     Note the correlation with age barely moves: the link between age and income")
print("     is still there in the rows you kept. That is what makes this bias hard to")
print("     spot - the model still 'works', it is just fitted to a younger population.")
print("   - Mean imputation keeps the mean by construction and CRUSHES the standard")
print("     deviation - it puts hundreds of identical values at the centre.")
print("   - KNN and the iterative model use age and score to predict income, so they")
print("     recover the relationship far better - the lowest RMSE of the four.")
print("   Mean imputation is not 'neutral'. It invents confidence you do not have.")

print("\n4. Always record WHERE you imputed.")
df["income_was_missing"] = df["income"].isna().astype(int)
df["income_filled"] = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()
print(df.head(4).to_string(index=False))
print("   The indicator column lets a model learn that 'we did not know' is itself")
print(f"   informative - here it correlates {np.corrcoef(df['income_was_missing'], df['age'])[0,1]:.3f} with age.")

print("\n5. The leakage rule that invalidates results.")
print("   Fit the imputer on TRAIN ONLY, then apply it to test.")
train, test = df.iloc[:400], df.iloc[400:]
imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit(train[["income"]])
correct = imp.transform(test[["income"]]).ravel()
wrong = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()[400:]
print(f"   median learnt from train only : {imp.statistics_[0]:,.0f}")
print(f"   median learnt from ALL data   : {np.nanmedian(df['income']):,.0f}")
print(f"   the two fills differ on {int((correct != wrong).sum())} test rows")
print("   Fitting on everything leaks test information into training, and your score")
print("   comes out better than the model will ever do in production.")

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Outliers can wreck regressions, distort clustering, and hide real signal. But not every extreme value is wrong — some outliers are exactly what you want to study (fraud, rare diseases, high spenders). The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests outlier detection methods (IQR, z-score, Isolation Forest), and the strategies for handling them.

The IQR rule — quick visual detection

IQR OUTLIER RULE

Q1 = 25th percentile, Q3 = 75th percentile
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Outliers are values below Q1 - 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR.
This is the boxplot whisker rule.

Extreme outliers: 3×IQR instead of 1.5×IQR. 
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def iqr_bounds(series, k=1.5):
 q1, q3 = series.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
 iqr = q3 - q1
 return q1 - k * iqr, q3 + k * iqr

low, high = iqr_bounds(df['income'])
outliers = df[(df['income'] < low) | (df['income'] > high)]
print(f"Outliers: {len(outliers)} of {len(df)}")

# Visualize with boxplot — same rule
import seaborn as sns
sns.boxplot(data=df, y='income')
# Points beyond whiskers are IQR outliers

# IQR rule pros:
# - Works for any distribution
# - Robust to outliers themselves (uses quantiles, not mean/std)
# - Intuitive: matches boxplot visualization

# IQR rule cons:
# - Fixed at 1.5× — may not match domain meaning
# - For very skewed data, lots of legit values flagged

Z-score — for roughly normal data

from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

# z = (x - mean) / std
# Flag if |z| > threshold (commonly 3)

z_scores = np.abs(stats.zscore(df['income']))
outliers = df[z_scores > 3]

# Or manually
mean = df['income'].mean()
std = df['income'].std()
df['income_z'] = (df['income'] - mean) / std
outliers = df[df['income_z'].abs() > 3]

# Caveats:
# - Mean and std are themselves sensitive to outliers (paradox)
# - Only meaningful for roughly normal data
# - For skewed data, z-score misses real outliers and over-flags tails

# Modified z-score using MEDIAN and MAD (robust)
median = df['income'].median()
mad = (df['income'] - median).abs().median()
df['income_mz'] = 0.6745 * (df['income'] - median) / mad
outliers = df[df['income_mz'].abs() > 3.5]
# More robust to skew and outliers in the data itself

Percentile-based

# Flag top 1% / bottom 1%
low, high = df['income'].quantile([0.01, 0.99])
outliers = df[(df['income'] < low) | (df['income'] > high)]

# Simple, intuitive, controllable — but always flags exactly the same fraction
# Useful when you know roughly what fraction should be outliers

# Different per-tail
low = df['income'].quantile(0.001) # very tight at bottom
high = df['income'].quantile(0.99) # 1% at top
outliers = df[(df['income'] < low) | (df['income'] > high)]

Multivariate outlier detection — Isolation Forest

from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# A row can be "normal" on every column but unusual as a COMBINATION
# Example: age=10 OK; age=10 + has-mortgage=True is suspicious

# Scale features first (distance-based)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X[['age', 'income', 'tenure_years', 'monthly_spend']])

iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.01, random_state=42)
labels = iso.fit_predict(X_scaled) # 1 = normal, -1 = outlier

df['is_outlier'] = (labels == -1)
print(f"Outliers flagged: {df['is_outlier'].sum()}")

# Continuous anomaly score
scores = iso.decision_function(X_scaled)
df['anomaly_score'] = -scores # higher = more anomalous

Handling outliers — five strategies

StrategyWhen to use
KeepOutliers may be legitimate (high spenders, rare diseases) — let the model see them
Cap (winsorize)Limit influence without dropping — preserves row count
Transformlog/sqrt/Box-Cox — compresses long tail naturally
RemoveOnly when you're sure they're data entry errors
Use robust modelsTrees, random forests, robust regression — built-in resistance to outliers

Capping / winsorizing

import numpy as np

# Cap at fixed percentiles
def cap(series, lower=0.01, upper=0.99):
 low = series.quantile(lower)
 high = series.quantile(upper)
 return series.clip(low, high)

df['income_capped'] = cap(df['income'])

# Cap at IQR bounds
def cap_iqr(series, k=1.5):
 q1, q3 = series.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
 iqr = q3 - q1
 return series.clip(q1 - k*iqr, q3 + k*iqr)

# scipy.stats.mstats.winsorize
from scipy.stats import mstats
df['income_w'] = mstats.winsorize(df['income'], limits=[0.01, 0.01])

# Pros: preserves all rows; reduces outlier impact
# Cons: changes the distribution; loses some real information
# Document the cap values for reproducibility

Log transform — natural compression for right-skew

import numpy as np

# Right-skewed positive data: income, price, count, time-to-event
df['log_income'] = np.log1p(df['income']) # log(1+x) handles zeros

# After log:
# - Distribution closer to symmetric
# - Outliers compressed (a $10M income is now log(10M) ≈ 16 vs 5 for log($100))
# - Linear models like ratios → "% change in y per % change in x"

from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer

pt = PowerTransformer(method='yeo-johnson') # handles negative values
X_trans = pt.fit_transform(X[['income', 'spend']])

# method='box-cox' requires strictly positive data
# Yeo-Johnson is the modern default

Data validation — schema-based checks

# Define expected ranges, types, allowed values
schema = {
 'age': {'type': 'int', 'min': 0, 'max': 120},
 'income': {'type': 'float', 'min': 0, 'max': 10_000_000},
 'city': {'type': 'str', 'allowed': ['NYC', 'LA', 'Chicago', 'Houston']},
 'date': {'type': 'datetime', 'min': '2020-01-01', 'max': '2025-12-31'}
}

# Manual validation
violations = []
for col, rules in schema.items():
 if 'min' in rules:
 violations.append((col, 'below_min', (df[col] < rules['min']).sum()))
 if 'max' in rules:
 violations.append((col, 'above_max', (df[col] > rules['max']).sum()))
 if 'allowed' in rules:
 bad = ~df[col].isin(rules['allowed'])
 violations.append((col, 'not_allowed', bad.sum()))

pd.DataFrame(violations, columns=['column', 'rule', 'violation_count'])

Outlier detection in time series — different rules

import pandas as pd

# Rolling z-score — outliers RELATIVE to local context
def rolling_zscore(s, window=30):
 rolling_mean = s.rolling(window).mean()
 rolling_std = s.rolling(window).std()
 return (s - rolling_mean) / rolling_std

df['z'] = rolling_zscore(df['temperature'])
outliers = df[df['z'].abs() > 3]

# Useful when:
# - Series has trend (raw z-score flags entire periods)
# - Series has seasonality (winter values look anomalous globally)
# - You want to flag changes relative to recent history

Worked example — full outlier audit

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Audit and handle outliers
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Step 1: per-column IQR audit
def iqr_audit(df, numeric_cols):
 results = []
 for col in numeric_cols:
 q1, q3 = df[col].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
 iqr = q3 - q1
 low, high = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr
 outliers = ((df[col] < low) | (df[col] > high)).sum()
 results.append({
 'col': col,
 'q1': q1, 'q3': q3, 'iqr': iqr,
 'low_bound': low, 'high_bound': high,
 'outlier_count': outliers,
 'outlier_pct': outliers / len(df) * 100
 })
 return pd.DataFrame(results)

audit = iqr_audit(df, ['age', 'income', 'tenure'])
print(audit)

# Step 2: handle differently per column
# Age: cap to (0, 120) — physiological limit
df['age'] = df['age'].clip(0, 120)

# Income: log transform — heavy right skew
df['log_income'] = np.log1p(df['income'])

# Tenure: keep but flag — long-tenure customers are real and important
df['tenure_outlier'] = (df['tenure'] > df['tenure'].quantile(0.99)).astype(int)

# Step 3: multivariate check
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df[['age', 'log_income', 'tenure']])
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.01, random_state=42)
df['multivariate_outlier'] = (iso.fit_predict(X_scaled) == -1).astype(int)

# Step 4: report
print(f"Univariate outliers (any column): {audit['outlier_count'].sum()}")
print(f"Multivariate outliers: {df['multivariate_outlier'].sum()}")
print(f"Overlap: {(df['multivariate_outlier'] == 1).sum()}")

# Document what was capped, transformed, flagged
# Don't drop anything without manual review

Common outlier-handling mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Dropping outliers automatically — often legitimate signal (fraud, premium customers)
  2. Using z-score on skewed data — IQR or percentile is more robust
  3. Using mean/std (sensitive to outliers) to flag outliers
  4. Capping then log-transforming — usually one or the other, not both
  5. Capping on the test set separately — caps should be computed on training data
  6. Using same threshold for all columns — different columns have different scales
  7. Treating extreme values as ALWAYS wrong — verify with domain knowledge
  8. Univariate-only checks on multivariate problems — Isolation Forest catches what column-wise misses
  9. No documentation of what was capped/dropped — irreproducible
  10. Z-score using corrupted std — std itself inflated by outliers; use median+MAD instead
★ ON THE EXAM

"IQR formula?" → Q3 - Q1.

"IQR outliers?" → Below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR.

"Z-score threshold?" → 3 is standard for "outlier".

"Robust z-score?" → Use median and MAD instead of mean and std.

"Winsorize?" → Cap values at percentiles: s.clip(low, high).

"Log transform purpose?" → Compress right-skewed positive distributions.

"log1p?" → log(1 + x); handles zero values safely.

"Box-Cox?" → Auto-find best transform; positive data only.

"Yeo-Johnson?" → Like Box-Cox but handles any real value.

"Multivariate outlier detection?" → Isolation Forest, LOF, One-Class SVM.

"Schema validation library?" → pandera, Great Expectations.

"Always before flagging outliers?" → Check distribution; choose method based on shape.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • IQR rule (Q1 − 1.5×IQR, Q3 + 1.5×IQR) is the standard univariate outlier method — robust to any distribution
  • Z-score (|z| > 3) only works on roughly normal data; use modified z-score with median+MAD for skewed
  • Percentile capping is intuitive but always flags the same fraction
  • Isolation Forest detects MULTIVARIATE outliers — combinations that are unusual together
  • Five handling strategies: keep, cap (winsorize), transform (log/Box-Cox), remove, use robust models
  • Cap with series.clip(low, high) to preserve row count while reducing influence
  • Log transform is the simplest fix for right-skewed positive distributions
  • Yeo-Johnson handles negative values; Box-Cox requires positive
  • For time-series, use rolling z-score (local context) instead of global statistics
  • Schema validation tools (pandera, Great Expectations) catch outliers automatically in production
  • Always document what was capped, transformed, or dropped — and why
  • Compute caps on training data only; apply same caps to test data (no peeking)
  • Outliers aren't always wrong — verify with domain knowledge before removing
  • Tree-based models tolerate outliers natively; linear models often need handling
